articles.title_orig: What to know about the online banking delays that affected major US banks
articles.title_zh: What to know about the online banking delays that affected major US banks
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of Chase Bank customers reported they had trouble using their online accounts on Monday.
“JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug,” a spokesperson said Monday. “It is taking longer than usual to service some customers.”
The Chase spokesperson went on to say it was a “bug,” rather than a widespread cyberattack.
Social media users reported issues with transactions at physical Chase branches, as well, and some local bank branches told customers earlier in the day that they were having issues with their internal system. However, Chase said in a statement that “customers still have access to their accounts and funds.”
The outage wasn’t caused by a cloud-related issue or a cyber attack, a source familiar with the matter told CNN. Rather, an update on the company’s own physical computer systems inadvertently caused issues.
As of 2:00 p.m. ET, more than 4,700 customers reported issues with Chase, according to Downdetector.
Customers reported issues at other major banks, including Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and U.S. Bank, though on a smaller scale.
The reports with the other banks appear to be related to sending money through Zelle, a digital payment network, to Chase accounts.
“U.S. Bank systems are not directly impacted. However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays,” U.S. Bank said in a statement.
Bank of America also said it was operating normally on Monday.
“Clients experiencing delays with other providers may wish to contact them directly for the latest information,” a spokesperson told CNN.
Zelle said that its service is “operating as it should.” The money-transferring service is owned by a consortium of US banks called Early Warning Services, and Zelle said it does not hold consumer funds.
“An issue at the financial institutions may be impacting broader services, including Zelle payments, for some of their customers,” a Zelle spokesperson said.
Chase also said it wasn’t a systemic issue.
“Other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us,” the spokesperson continued.
Monday’s Chase outage marked the third straight weekday with a massive technical failure.
On Thursday, a Microsoft outage cut off email access to millions of people across 74 countries and territories. On Friday, a Federal Aviation Administration systems failure led to a nationwide ground stop .
And on Monday afternoon, United Airlines reported a systemwide computer problem that delayed flights.
The incidents don’t share the same scope or root causes. Microsoft blamed a Windows defect, a traffic overload and capacity constraints. The FAA cited a router deployment issue and excessive data flooding its systems. It’s not yet clear what caused the Chase or United outages on Monday.
But the glitches share a common theme: “the complexity and fragility of the systems that we depend on every day,” Mike Chapple, a professor of IT, Analytics, and Operations at the University of Notre Dame, said in emailed comments.
“In each of these cases, what started as an issue in one small part of a larger system quickly spread, causing massive disruptions nationwide,” he added.
Complexity and interdependence aren’t inherently flaws — in fact, they make systems more resilient, noted Rebecca Krauthamer, CEO and cofounder of QuSecure, a cryptography provider for the US government.
“But when dependencies on systems aren’t sufficiently understood, failures can cascade across institutions and industries,” she added.
Think about it like the Titanic: The watertight bulkheads were unable to withstand a failure that exceeded the ship’s architects’ worst-case-scenario assumptions. Even the best-designed systems sometimes succumb to threats and problems that the designers couldn’t have imagined when they built them.
The problem with interdependent technology systems is that system failures are rarely isolated incidents: Our heavy reliance on a handful of systems means failures have tended to bring down systems across the world.
“The question for leaders is not whether one system will fail but how many other things fail with it, and how fast you can contain it,” said Madhu Shashanka, founder of Concentric AI.
This story has been updated with additional developments.
CNN’s David Goldman contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: UK sanctions firms over Israeli West Bank settlements
articles.title_zh: UK sanctions firms over Israeli West Bank settlements
articles.content_orig:
Foreign affairs minister Penny Wong says rapid expansion of settlements and settler violence are ‘extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution’
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
Australia has announced another tranche of sanctions on individuals and organisations involved in illegal settlement expansion and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the West Bank .
In a statement, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong , said it was the first time Australian sanctions had targeted a construction company involved in the building of settlements.
The sanctions prohibit Australians and Australian businesses from trading with or providing financial or other support to three individuals and four organisations.
“We are taking these actions because the rapid expansion of settlements and settler violence are extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution,” Wong’s statement said.
“This includes the E1 settlement where demolitions and the displacement of Palestinians have occurred in recent weeks. Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law.”
Among those sanctioned is Daniella Weiss and her Israeli settler organisation, the Nachala movement, which the government said has provided support for outposts and settlements that have perpetrated serious human rights abuses.
Weiss is known as the “godmother” of the settler movement and was sanctioned by the UK in May 2025, shortly after she appeared on a Louis Theroux’s documentary The Settlers .
Prominent West Bank settler Eliav Libi has also been sanctioned, as well as the Eyal Hari Yehuda construction company which has helped develop settlements and outposts and demolished Palestinian structures in the West Bank.
Wong said the sanctioned individuals and organisations had “actively participated in the planning, coordination and establishment of new settlements, including raising funds, recruitment of volunteers and providing support to violent settlers”.
Speaking on ABC radio on Wednesday morning, Wong said Australia had been coordinating with the UK on the sanctions.
“We thought it was very important to work with the United Kingdom to have a coordinated set of sanctions ahead of those decisions.
“We urge Israel to desist from proceeding with this settlement, which renders likely unviable the prospect of a Palestinian state.”
Wong said she had spoken to her Israeli counterpart, Gideon Sa’ar, on Tuesday night when she “outlined” Australia’s position.
“We’ve made clear we will continue to take action in respect of those involved in the settlement enterprise. The settlement enterprise is violent.”
after newsletter promotion
Wong had signalled further sanctions in September, after the government ruled out an import ban on trade from illegal settlements in the West Bank.
On Wednesday, the foreign affairs minister said the government was still considering further action, but provided no detail.
“We’ll continue to look at targeted measures we can take to push back against what the current Israeli government is doing,” Wong told journalists.
When asked whether Wong was concerned Israel would respond to Australia sanctions with countermeasures, the minister said it had in the past.
“We’ve seen the Israeli government take action against Australia, including asking our diplomats to leave Ramallah. We’ve also seen the caretaker prime minister, Netanyahu, be very public in his criticism of Australia.
“So obviously, there is a reaction to Australia acting, but we think this is the right thing to do.”
The statement warned Australian businesses they must not bid for construction tenders for illegal settlement developments.
Individuals breaching sanctions can attract a penalty of up to 10 years’ imprisonment and a fine of up to $910,000 or three times the value of the relevant transaction.
Businesses can be fined up to $3.64m or three times the value of the relevant transaction.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft unveils AI models for coding, cybersecurity as it takes on Anthropic, OpenAI
articles.title_zh: Microsoft unveils AI models for coding, cybersecurity as it takes on Anthropic, OpenAI
articles.content_orig:
Satya Nadella, Microsoft Chairman and CEO, delivered the opening keynote at Ignite in San Francisco this morning. Here is an edited version of his remarks.
This week is about two things: First is how we capitalize on new capabilities that are growing exponentially. And second is how do we build the capability to deal with the consequences of these exponentials.
At times like these, I always find it helpful to be grounded in our mission: To empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more. In today’s world, that means building a frontier ecosystem. We need to parlay any technological advance into real outcomes and new points of leverage for people, organizations and society at large.
For us, that comes down to three things: Keeping human ambition at the center, ensuring your control of your organization’s intelligence and learning, and trust.
And so, our goal is to build a stack that addresses these three core architectural principles.
Copilot is the new OS for work . Copilot brings together all the new form factors of human-computer interaction, whether it is Chat, Cowork, Code or Autopilot, into one experience. It also brings together the disparate categories of knowledge work, coding and business process. That is why we have all of Office with its richness built into Copilot. And underlying it is a model system that matches the right intelligence to the right context to the right form factor to accomplish the task.
Home gives you one place to start, whether you need a quick answer or want to assign and complete complex, multi-step tasks. Code brings the power of an infinite SaaS factory to every individual. It lets you build your own custom SaaS apps, dashboards and much more. And Autopilot is an autonomous agent that keeps moving your work forward 24×7 in all the places where you and your team collaborate.
Underlying all this is Work IQ. You can think of this as the most important database for any organization, with a deep understanding of people, their relationships, documents, emails, meetings, chats and projects that make up the fabric of work.
And we are going further. We are extending Copilot for specific roles: sales, legal, finance, service. We are organizing the skills, connectors and plugins for these roles across the entire surface area of Copilot.
And that includes third-party systems, too. In fact, today we are announcing new plugins for business applications, starting with Dynamics 365. And it is not just Dynamics. We are very excited to partner with Salesforce to bring Salesforce to Copilot .
And we are going beyond that as well. Up until now, we have mostly been in a single player world of people and their agent loops and swarms. But the time has come for a true multiplayer form factor, where people, their agents and other people are all driving towards a common goal, with shared context. This is Copilot Workspaces:
The idea behind IQ is to help every organization build, retain and continuously improve its own intelligence. Essentially, we are taking the system we built underneath Copilot and externalizing it as a first-class platform that embodies your organizational intelligence as an asset that you continuously build and control.
We are bringing together all of the data you have across Fabric, Foundry and Microsoft 365. And, of course, all the third-party context too. Microsoft IQ comes with hundreds of new connectors we are announcing today, so agents can get the full enterprise context where business gets done. And all this rich context manifests as business plugins that can be shared and inherited across the organization.
For us, it is about mapping intelligence to a given task, with the best economics. This is something we can uniquely do in the context of real-world tasks by tuning our products, harness and tools, and the model system, end-to-end.
And today we are thrilled to announce Microsoft-Decision-1.1 , which is now generally available and ready for enterprise deployment. We have added multimodal support. And we have improved performance, making decisions more accurate and responses faster. Already, more than 4,000 customers have used it. And we ourselves are using it for core tasks like routing, data labeling, personalization, content filtering and hundreds of other use cases.
Foundry of course has all the most popular closed and open weight models, too. We are very excited to bring GPT 6.2 to Foundry. It is a great model that sets a new bar for AI in professional work. And today we are announcing that Meta’s latest models are all coming to Foundry as well.
We are also innovating at the frontier with our own MAI model family that is both compute-efficient when it comes to pre-training and token-efficient when it comes to product deployment. Our goal is to put additional points on the frontier curve informed by real world task-performance.
And we are going further. We are announcing MAI Licensed Weights, meaning our trusted customers will now be able to get access to Microsoft AI model weights through our Frontier Co.
Today, we are introducing lots of new models . But I want to highlight two in particular:
First, Code. We are introducing our new flagship family of agentic coding models: Code 2. Code 2 is at the frontier of cost-performance for everyday enterprise coding tasks. It excels in taking code to production, deep debugging, multifile implementation, repo-wide reasoning and UI at a fraction of frontier cost.
Code 2 Flash is designed for fast, high-volume work like code explanations, targeted edits, routine fixes and rapid iterations. It brings near-flagship quality for a much lower cost. These models are both generally available today on GitHub Copilot, both in the model picker and as part of Copilot Fusion. They are also available in Foundry.
We are taking the same approach in cyber. Cyber 2 Flash is our most capable security model yet. It is a flash-sized model that delivers performance ahead of frontier models at a fraction of the cost per task. And, just as we have done with coding, we are co-designing the model with the tools and systems where it will be used. We are integrating Cyber 2 with Perception.
Successfully deploying AI systems starts with making sure you have observability at every layer of the stack. That is where Agent 365 comes in. It is a control plane that extends your existing governance, identity, security and management systems to the agents in your enterprise. We already have over 50 million agents in Agent 365.
And it includes FinOps, too. As AI scales, every organization needs a clear line between what it spends and the value AI creates. That is why today we are announcing Agent 365 Business Analytics. You can think of it as your ERP system for AI usage. You can see exactly what is driving spend. You can connect spend to outcomes to drive business value. And you can optimize ROI across different scenarios.
The next thing I want to talk about is how you take the environment you have set up, from Copilot to IQ to Agent 365, and secure it. And that is where Perception and our security stack comes in. We are building an end-to-end trust platform. We are helping customers both secure their AI deployments and use AI to strengthen their security posture.
Perception is a complete agentic security system with teams of red, blue and green agents that run through playbooks to deliver security outcomes at machine speed, with you always in control.
Essentially, think about it like this: red team agents simulate attacks, blue team agents detect attacks and green team agents fix and remediate. With Playbooks, you can compose teams of agents to tackle complex jobs and trigger them to take action autonomously.
Perception helps connect all the signals, sensors and actuators across your identity, client, cloud, apps and agents to intelligence to secure your end-to-end environments. And I am very excited to share that Perception is now generally available.

articles.content_orig:
Waymo driverless vehicles are banned from operating on all California freeways, the state’s Department of Motor Vehicles said Tuesday, citing public safety concerns following a series of accidents involving the vehicles.
The agency said the autonomous cars pose “imminent hazard to public safety” following at least two incidents in which the vehicles drove into construction zones.
This is the second time this year Waymo has faced highway restrictions in the state, according to CNN affiliate KGO . The company paused freeway operations in May in San Francisco and Los Angeles to improve its vehicles’ response to construction zones.
The restriction went into effect on November 11 and will remain in effect until Waymo addresses the safety lapses, the agency said.
This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title_orig: The data is very preliminary, but Vulcan failure may not be due to BE-4 engines
articles.title_zh: The data is very preliminary, but Vulcan failure may not be due to BE-4 engines
articles.content_orig:
United Launch Alliance (ULA) confirmed Tuesday morning that its return-to-flight launch of the Vulcan rocket began failing during the initial stages of the mission.
“While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff, the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit,” the company said .
The launch company also confirmed reporting by Ars that the Centaur V upper stage and the solid rocket boosters performed nominally during the flight.
Critically, ULA did not provide any specific information about the “low booster performance.” This matters greatly because the core stage of the Vulcan rocket is powered by two BE-4 engines, which are provided by Blue Origin. That company’s own New Glenn rocket uses a similar but slightly more powerful version of the BE-4 engine. And New Glenn experienced its own catastrophic failure in May during a ground test, a failure that later was attributed to a main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines.
Information about the Vulcan failure is being closely held by ULA and Blue Origin, who have only acknowledged that they’re working together to investigate the cause. According to two sources, the investigation is “incredibly complicated” and remains in the early stages.
However, according to preliminary data, two independent sources indicated to Ars that the problem is currently believed to have originated on the launch vehicle side rather than in the engines themselves. The issue may be related to systems that feed methane and liquid oxygen propellant to the engines.
ULA engineers are looking at the possibility that one of the two BE-4 engines started producing lower thrust shortly after liftoff and never ramped back up to full throttle for the remainder of the burn. Video observations from high-zoom tracking cameras appeared to show one engine slightly dimmer than the other after Vulcan jettisoned its solid rocket boosters nearly two minutes into flight. An asymmetric shutdown of the BE-4 engines could also have contributed to the sudden attitude motion indicated by ULA’s telemetry-driven real-time animation near stage separation.
The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the investigation, which is being led by ULA. Again, this information is preliminary, and no definitive conclusions can or should be drawn.
This was the fifth flight of the Vulcan rocket since its debut in January 2024. Two of the previous flights have experienced issues with the nozzles on its solid rocket boosters, but in both cases, the rocket was able to compensate for the reduced and asymmetric thrust and reach its intended orbit. The second nozzle issue caused Vulcan to stand down for nine months.
This latest setback is likely to sideline Vulcan for at least half a year, and probably longer. Most impacted will be the US Space Force, which has national security payloads waiting for a ride to space on Vulcan, and Amazon, which had more than a dozen launches of its Amazon Leo constellation on the manifest for 2027. It would exacerbate a worsening launch crisis in the United States.
There are potentially serious implications for Blue Origin as well, which is seeking to return New Glenn to flight as early as January. Last Tuesday, the company said a modified BE-4 main oxygen valve had successfully completed qualification testing.
“Our modified valve has already been incorporated into engines slated for upcoming flights, and we are now rolling it out across the remaining fleet,” the company said . “We expect to complete the anomaly investigation later this month.”
If Vulcan’s failure were ultimately due to a problem with the BE-4 engine, it would certainly delay the New Glenn rocket’s return to flight. This would be a setback not just for Blue Origin but for NASA, which is counting on the super heavy lift rocket to do much of the heavy lifting for its Artemis Program and Moon Base.

articles.title_orig: The first pill to slow Alzheimer’s could come from an unexpected place
articles.title_zh: The first pill to slow Alzheimer’s could come from an unexpected place
articles.content_orig:
AriBio’s erectile dysfunction med-turned Alzheimer’s disease candidate mirodenafil has delivered some mixed results from a global phase 3 trial.
In patients with early Alzheimer’s disease, AriBio’s mirodenafil candidate, AR1001, delivered better clinical outcomes than placebo did—but only in a subgroup of patients who were not on any background therapies such as an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor or memantine, according to results from the Polaris-AD trial.
In the overall population, including those receiving other therapies at baseline, the trial missed statistical significance on change in the Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) at week 52. The data were shared at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer Disease conference in Boston.
The trial is technically positive, as it’s designed with dual primary populations, each with its separate statistical significance bar. AriBio said it plans to discuss the results with the FDA.
Digging into the readout, among 604 patients in the prespecified monotherapy population, AR1001 performed 0.44 points better versus placebo, with a p-value of 0.0266 meeting the prespecified statistical significance threshold of 0.03. This translated into a 31% slowing of clinical decline, according to AriBio. For the entire trial of 1,535 patients, the treatment difference came in at 0.11 points lower on CDR-SB in favor of AR1001, or a 7% slowing of decline, but the p-value reached 0.4015, failing the prespecified statistical significance bar of 0.02.
“We started developing AR1001 with the goal of creating an oral treatment that could slow Alzheimer’s progression and be practical for patients and care partners to use over the long term,” Jai-Jun Choung, Ph.D., chairman and CEO of AriBio, said in a Nov. 16 statement. “The 31% slowing of clinical decline at one year in the Monotherapy population supports our hypothesis.”
AR1001 showed numerical advantage on secondary cognitive and functional measures in the monotherapy population, including a treatment effect of 1.16 points versus placebo on the Alzheimer’s Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive Subscale 13 and a 0.7-point difference on the Mini-Mental State Examination.
With the phase 3 readout, the ball is now in Fosun Pharma’s court. The Chinese pharma paid South Korea’s AriBio $60 million in May for an option to potentially in-license AR1001, a PDE5 inhibitor like Viagra, in the U.S., Europe and Japan. Fosun has 90 days after receiving full Polaris-AD data to decide whether to exercise its option, which will trigger up to $180 million in upfront and regulatory milestone payments.
Originally developed by SK Chemicals Life Science, mirodenafil has been approved in Korea since 2007 for erectile dysfunction. AR1001 uses a lower dose of the drug at 30 mg taken daily. The drug works differently than antibodies such as Eisai and Biogen’s Leqembi and Eli Lilly’s Kisunla, which directly target amyloid-beta plaques in the brain.
By inhibiting PDE5, mirodenafil prevents the breakdown of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP), which promotes neuron survival and synaptic plasticity. As a brain-penetrant small molecule, the drug can also dilate cerebral blood vessels, potentially improving blood supply to the brain, while theoretically helping the brain clear toxic protein aggregates like amyloid-beta.
Supporting those mechanisms, the Polaris-AD trial showed that AR1001 increased cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cGMP levels versus placebo after one year in both the overall and monotherapy populations. CSF p-tau217 results numerically favored AR1001, but no difference in the CSF Aβ42/40 ratio, which evaluates the presence of amyloid plaque, was observed.
It’s difficult to compare AR1001’s data with anti-amyloid antibodies because of different trial designs. Previously, in the phase 3 Clarity AD trial, Leqembi achieved a 0.45-point difference versus placebo on the CDR-SB metric at 18 months, slowing clinical decline by 27%. About 60% of patients in that study were taking symptomatic Alzheimer’s medications at baseline.
Both Clarity AD and Polaris-AD targeted patients with early symptomatic Alzheimer’s disease, although the baseline characteristics of cognitive impairment were different.
In an interview with Fierce in June, Fosun Pharma’s CEO of the firm's innovative medicines division, Xingli Wang, M.D., Ph.D., highlighted low dropouts from the Polaris-AD trial, as well as a high rollover rate into the trial's extension period, as positive signs.
In a Nov. 16 release, AriBio described AR1001 as “generally well tolerated.” Over the one-year double-blind treatment phase, serious adverse events happened in 10% of patients in the AR1001 arm, versus 9.8% in the control arm. Deaths happened in four (0.5%) of patients receiving AR1001 and two (0.3%) receiving placebo. Adverse events led to discontinuation of study drug in 5.2% of AR1001-treated participants and 1.7% of placebo-treated participants.
“Polaris-AD has given us important phase 3 data, including results in the prespecified monotherapy population, as well as safety data, for a once-daily oral therapy that could offer patients a convenient treatment option,” Wang said in a Nov. 16 statement. “We will remain patient-centered and, based on the complete body of evidence, continue to work closely with AriBio on the full dataset.”
“The CDR-SB finding in the prespecified monotherapy population and the safety profile are encouraging. The secondary endpoints and biomarker findings warrant further evaluation alongside the overall population outcome to understand AR1001’s therapeutic effects in early Alzheimer’s disease,” Sharon Sha, M.D., of Stanford University and principal investigator of Polaris-AD, said in a statement. “The work of Polaris-AD is another step towards filling an unmet need in early Alzheimer’s disease in which patients need more options for treatment.”

articles.title_orig: Is Apple down? Thousands report problems accessing services
articles.title_zh: Is Apple down? Thousands report problems accessing services
articles.content_orig:
Apple said an internal update was to blame for a major outage on Nov. 17 that hit its App Store, iCloud, Apple Pay and other software, with thousands of users reporting problems online.
In a statement to USA TODAY, Apple said it was working to fix the affected systems, and services are expected to return to normal soon.
"Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We're working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible," the company said.
Apple, on its System Status page , confirmed outages on App Store, Apple Music and AppleCare on Device, as well as issues with iCloud Account & Sign In. The company told Bloomberg the problems weren't caused by a cyberattack.
According to outage tracker Downdetector, reports of issues with Apple Pay began to spike at around 11:40 a.m. ET with a peak of reports at around 12:15 p.m. ET. Outage reports for iCloud also started to surge just before noon ET, though reports on Downdetector don't reflect every user experiencing a problem. Those reports had dropped significantly by mid-afternoon.
The Apple software issues came on the heels of a major banking outage on Nov. 16 that stemmed from Chase Bank. It also impacted Wells Fargo, Bank of America, online payment platform Zelle and other institutions.
Last week, a communications outage disrupted air traffic across the United States, and a Microsoft outage prevented many from checking their Outlook email and accessing Microsoft 365 services like Teams and Word.

articles.title_orig: Europe fears what Trump, Xi and Putin might discuss behind closed doors in China
articles.title_zh: Europe fears what Trump, Xi and Putin might discuss behind closed doors in China
articles.content_orig:
Three strongman leaders over age 70, 90% of the world’s nuclear weapons, two ongoing wars, one room, and no specific agenda. What could possibly go wrong?
What Presidents Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping will discuss during their unprecedented trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday is far from concrete. But that is perhaps the point. A high-level summit like this would usually establish clear outcomes ahead of time, and be the culmination of months of intense planning and signalling.
But whatever preceded the Shenzhen meeting matters little with the inclusion of a wild card like Trump. Nuclear non-proliferation was flagged as a main focus, though little progress is expected – to say nothing of “safeguarding world peace,” another agenda item according to China. Then suddenly, Trump mentioned Iran, Ukraine, Nvidia, and even floated a meeting with North Korea’s Kim Jong Un.
It’s not abnormal for world leaders to go off script. Yet it has rarely been as risky as it will be Thursday. Especially when it comes to Ukraine.
Trump referred to Europe’s longest ongoing war Monday with both a slip of a tongue and sarcasm. He called Ukraine “my favorite subject” and added, “Ukraine’s losing – Ukraine-Russia is losing 25,000 soldiers a month” – almost edging Russia’s horrific losses out of his sentence. Ukraine is for Trump the irritant that got itself invaded, hasn’t accepted his hurried and compromising peace, and is always losing.
The Shenzhen meeting is a risky moment not because Kyiv and its European allies will suddenly buckle under whatever declarations emerge; they have grown sufficiently inured to Washington’s fickle nature. The danger is in Trump’s desire to be liked by powerful authoritarians, what is agreed to in private, and how that informs Putin’s confidence and Xi’s perception of Trump’s mental health.
Putin has, for free, got his moment on the world stage, allowing him to present Russia, for a day, as the global superpower it once was, rather than the one it is brutally struggling to become again.
Anxiety among European officials is palpable. “Trump listens to the last person he talks to, so that will be a driver for what he says,” said one European official speaking to CNN on the condition of anonymity. A European diplomat said it was: “Hard to see anything good on European security to come out of this meeting.”
Another senior European official said the optics of the trilateral were “of course awful for us,” but was less concerned a wider deal would be struck.
The first official called the meeting a “Putin dream,” ushering in his rehabilitation on the world stage, and added a key issue for Trump would be “who stands in the middle of the big boys takeaway picture.”
That picture of the three leaders after their meeting will speak a thousand words about Western decline. The man who invaded Ukraine unprovoked nearly five years ago, his bankroller in chief, and the US president who has reversed decades of US policy to pressure Kyiv to accept a bad deal, through limiting military aid.
A key risk is Trump agreeing with a Russian narrative, or fictional presentation of the frontline facts, and feeling obliged to adhere to a deal he has hurriedly made with the two strongmen he not-so-secretly admires.
Many of the European officials CNN spoke to harbor distant hopes that Beijing may emerge as a good-faith arbiter in the war. It is a view born of Xi’s apparent pressure on Putin to curtail nuclear saber-rattling , China’s stopping short of the full-scale arming of Russia during the war, and Beijing’s ambition to become the global superpower that can enforce effective change.
But this rosy view overlooks how urgently China needs Moscow to not lose this war, to prevent another key ally from suffering humiliation, and how the US has ridden roughshod over Iran and Venezuela this year – two Chinese allies whose degradation Beijing might like to see avenged by the collective West suffering a defeat in Ukraine.
The past month has delivered repeated blows to Ukraine and European NATO countries, dressed in the guise of the US peace process, led by Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, and friend Steve Witkoff, two envoys who have limited diplomatic experience and even less diplomatic successes to their names. First, Trump struck a deal to buy Russian diesel, wiping away years of sanctions and opening the door to the replenishing of the Kremlin’s war chest. Then followed the mysterious stoppages in US intelligence sharing and Starshield services – vital to the nightly defense of Ukraine from Russian missiles – that the White House appears to have suggested either didn’t happen or shouldn’t have.
In a Kremlin meeting last month, Witkoff called Putin a “humanitarian” after he released retired American teacher and US military veteran Stephen Hubbard.
Then Kushner, after meeting Putin’s envoy in DC, recast the peace process as a bid for a new European security infrastructure, pandering to the Kremlin narrative that the real belligerent is NATO next door - and not Russia, who invaded one neighbour, Georgia in 2008, and another, Ukraine, twice in 2014 and 2022.
After further Starshield restrictions were placed on Ukraine during a peace summit, Kushner flew to Moscow hoping Putin would “give his blessing” to Europe joining the trilateral peace talks. He emerged saying Putin had done so, only to be flatly contradicted by the Kremlin. And finally, Kushner appears to have suggested NATO-type security guarantees if Ukraine gives up the rest of the Donbas region, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
And, this is just the stuff that is publicly known. It is not too far-fetched to see the Shenzhen summit as the pinnacle of Trump’s settling into Moscow’s orbit. His actions in public show no other course. He even suggested Putin could have been “a lot tougher” on Ukraine, a statement that can only nod to Russia’s nuclear arsenal, given its nightly exhausting of its conventional armaments into Ukraine’s skies.
This will not be a feared Yalta 2.0, in which global powers carve up the world. The first Yalta summit in 1945 divided the world after the worst conflict in its history, between three victors whose empires either crumbled or bloomed afterwards.
Different men will attend Shenzhen. Trump and Putin are fighting different and failing wars of choice, and are the aging embodiment of their nations’ waning power. Xi has overseen a brutal, staggeringly efficient and swift rise of a global tech superpower, but still flinches away from conflict in his own potential war of choice – the invasion of Taiwan.
History had no choice but to listen to Truman, Stalin and Churchill after World War II. It might choose to tune out Shenzhen.
But the damage need not come in the form of Trump parroting Kremlin talking points when he emerges. Or Putin being given a space on the world stage for his false historical lectures on Russian victimhood and supremacy. Or Xi – probably the largest-scale authoritarian in history – appearing to be the reasonable, calm one.
The gift to Moscow is in how little opposition Putin will feel. The two most powerful men in the world are likely to give him an easy ride in private, and not demand an immediate ceasefire or durable peace in Ukraine. Pressure will instead be focused on Ukrainian and European concessions. The peace process may suffer yet another curiously pro-Russian reset that buys the Kremlin months more to try and seize tiny pockets of the Donbas, or let Ukrainian mothers and children suffer through another freezing winter.
There is little time left for these aging leaders – Xi is 73, Putin is 74 and Trump is 80 – to change the world. Perhaps this is just a blip in the autocratic curve of history. But the ticking clock makes the remaining two years of this US presidency particularly perilous.

articles.title_orig: Outage math at the airport: When a four-hour Uber beats waiting out a ground stop
articles.title_zh: Outage math at the airport: When a four-hour Uber beats waiting out a ground stop
articles.content_orig:
By MELISSA KOENIG, US REPORTER and ASSOCIATED PRESS
Published: 17:12 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 08:04 EST, 17 November 2026
United Airlines flights across the United States were grounded on Monday night, just days after a technical issue prompted the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to ground all flights nationwide.
The airline announced on social media that it was experiencing a 'widespread system outage' as it apologized to customers 'for the inconvenience.'
'We're aware of the widespread system and our teams are working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible,' it posted on X.
'We appreciate your patience while we work through this,' the airline added, urging anyone with scheduled flights to keep checking their flight status on the app.
The post has since been deleted, as a spokesperson for the airline told the Daily Mail that the issue has been resolved.
'While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights,' the spokesperson said, adding: 'There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.'
The update came after frustrated travelers took to social media to bemoan how their flights could not take off.
'Currently stuck on the tarmac,' one X user posted, blaming it on an IT issue in which the airline 'can't clear planes for takeoff as [they] can't connect to the weight system.'
United Airlines flights across the country were grounded Monday night as the airline experienced a 'widespread system outage'
The issue comes just days after a technical issue prompted the Federal Aviation Administration to ground all flights nationwide
United Airlines said on social media its teams were 'working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible'
The outage is now the latest in a string of technical issues that have crippled businesses around the country and left airline passengers stranded for hours amid a rare nationwide ground stop.
Earlier Monday, thousands of customers with Chase, Bank of America, Capital One and Wells Fargo also flagged being unable to log in or transfer money , according to Down Detector, a website which tracks real-time user reports.
A spokesperson for Chase told the Daily Mail the outage was caused by a technical bug.
'Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,' they said. 'We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.'
Chase also addressed one complaint on X, telling a client: 'I do apologize, it appears that we are currently working to resolve an issue with online banking.
'Please try again at a later time. We're sorry for any inconvenience, and appreciate your patience.'
Wells Fargo also posted a note on its website telling customers that 'online banking isn't available right now' due to 'technical issues'.
A spokesperson for Chase later noted that the technical problems were not the result of a cyberattack.
'JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system - it is not cyber-related,' said spokesman Joe Evangelisti.
In the same statement, Evangelisti said that this was a Chase-only issue.
'This is not a systemic issue - other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us,' he said.
Customers at three major US banks have been locked out of their accounts as Chase and Wells Fargo all experienced outages on Monday afternoon
Over 20,000 flights were canceled from Friday to Sunday, according to airline tracker FlightAware. During that same period, over 25,000 flights were delayed, and lingering impacts have bled into Monday
A spokesman for US Bank said its systems were not directly impacted but that 'clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.'
Zelle is the peer-to-peer payment system that major US banks use to allow customers to send money to friends and family at near-instant speed.
It is owned by Arizona-based Early Warning Services, which in turn is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, US Bank and Wells Fargo.
A spokesman for Early Warning Services said the Zelle network was fully operational.
'An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers,' the spokesman said.
Still, the outage sparked panic as it came just three days after Microsoft experienced widespread issues on Friday , leaving people unable to access Outlook, Teams and Copilot applications.
Businesses ground to a halt, healthcare providers lost contact with patients, courts lost live feeds, and governments struggled to communicate.
The suspected cause was a faulty network configuration change that resulted in numerous servers becoming unavailable, overloading the remaining infrastructure.
The FAA also issued a rare nationwide ground stop at all US airports following a major communications failure on Friday.
'What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack,' Trump said on Monday of the FAA outage that forced thousands of cancelled and delayed flights over the weekend
The Air Traffic Control System Command Center (ATCSCC) said on Friday that the  halting of 3,500 US flights for five hours was 'due to extraordinary circumstances for safety reasons'.
'There has been a temporary telecommunications outage - out of an abundance of caution, all flights have been halted,' the FAA said.
'Every flight has been accounted for, and international flights will be handled on a case-by-case basis.'
President Donald Trump has since blamed half-century-old aviation equipment for the ground stop, which led to thousands of cancellations and travel woes for over a million passengers.
'We have old, broken equipment,' the President said Monday at the White House before departing for his trip to Asia on board the new Air Force One plane gifted to the administration by Qatari officials.
He noted that some of the equipment that went down was 55 years old.
'We essentially want to blow it up and put new in, and we can do it simultaneously with very little trouble. What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack.'
The incident marked only the second time since the 9/11 terrorist attacks that a nationwide ground stop was implemented.
The stoppage also prevented any domestic flights from taking off, resulting in one of the worst travel snarls in recent US history. It began around 3.30pm and was not lifted until around 8.20pm.
More than 20,000 flights were canceled from Friday to Sunday, according to airline tracker FlightAware. During that same period, over 25,000 flights were delayed, and lingering impacts have bled into Monday.
It is estimated that more than one million American travelers have been impacted by the outage.
Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy claimed Biden-era upgrades were shoddy
The President also cast blame on his predecessor for the FAA glitch.
'The Biden administration hooked up a lot of copper into glass. And copper, if you know anything about electrical engineering, you cannot hook up copper into glass. So a lot of money was wasted, but the equipment is very old,' Trump said.
He was referring to Biden-era upgrades to communication systems built on copper wiring that were upgraded to fiber-optic, or glass, wires.
Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said the upgrade work was shoddy, resulting in the outage.
Trump said the upgrade was a waste of money and more cash would be needed from Congress to fully upgrade the system and prevent future issues.
'We want to make it beyond safe. We want to have the best system in the world, and for that we need Congress,' the President told reporters.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang Open to Return as Nvidia CEO, But Board Not Considering It
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang Open to Return as Nvidia CEO, But Board Not Considering It
articles.content_orig:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who abruptly stepped down last week after a scandal involving extramarital affairs, said Tuesday he would be “honored” to return to the role if the board were to allow it.
“I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret,” Huang said in a statement.
He stepped down last week from the company he co-founded 33 years ago, ending an extraordinary run at the helm of one of the world’s most valuable companies.
The resignation came just four days after the company’s board announced it was investigating him, following reports that he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, who sources have identified as a potential Chinese intelligence asset; as well as reports of another affair with an Nvidia executive.
CNN’s numerous attempts to reach Alice Huang for comment have been unsuccessful.
“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Jensen Huang said in the statement, noting support he’s received.
CNN has reached out to Nvidia for comment on Huang’s statement. The company’s board of directors, however, is not considering reinstating Huang, a source familiar with the situation told CNN.
President Donald Trump, who frequently looked to Huang for guidance on the nation’s AI policies, said Monday he “would not mind” if Huang returned as CEO. Trump is scheduled to meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping later in the week. The president said he “may” discuss Nvidia with Xi.
Beyond Trump, Huang has seen a strong showing of support in recent days – both from current and former Nvidia employees and across Silicon Valley. Elon Musk said in a post on X that he would be “honored” to hire Huang. The Tesla and SpaceX CEO also said he would be signing a growing petition for Nvidia’s board to bring back Huang.
The US intelligence community is still working to understand the relationship between Alice Huang and the Chinese government. Multiple sources have told CNN that the intelligence collected on her to date does not prove that she was acting as a spy for Beijing.
Nvidia is synonymous with the global AI boom, supplying some of the most advanced chips that power AI models for some of the world’s largest technology companies. On Thursday, Nvidia announced its Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as the company’s interim CEO while the board considers internal and external candidates.
Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before Congress in a hearing scheduled for December 1, and Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, will testify the following day. Both will be closed-door hearings with transcribed interviews subsequently released to the public.
Huang previously apologized to his family and Nvidia employees in a company message last week, acknowledging that he had been unfaithful to his wife and saying he would cooperate with an independent investigation initiated by the company’s board of directors.
“I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security,” he said last week.
Alice Huang is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based tech company and Nvidia customer.
Some US sources say that whether or not she was recruited by China’s intelligence service, she posed a counterintelligence risk because Chinese national security law requires its citizens to assist in intelligence-gathering efforts if asked. Concerns have been mounting that chips Megaspeed purchased were diverted to Chinese entities, potentially skirting US export restrictions.
Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing, saying it is a “compliant and legal company” and that it will cooperate with the US investigation. In a statement to CNN, Nvidia said allegations of illegal chip diversion were “thoroughly investigated and debunked last year.”
China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs called the allegations that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy “groundless speculation and an attempt to smear and malign China.”
Nvidia is scheduled to report its third-quarter earnings later on Tuesday and hold a subsequent call with analysts, which will be the first opportunity for the public to hear directly from the company’s new leadership.

articles.title_orig: Three China-related Items to Consider as Trump Again Meets with Xi
articles.title_zh: Three China-related Items to Consider as Trump Again Meets with Xi
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
SEOUL — President Trump will get his wish for a historic meeting among the three most powerful men in the world — Xi Jinping of China, Vladimir Putin of Russia and himself — at a summit Thursday in southern China.
But Moscow, Beijing and Washington already know their leaders are arriving at the Shenzhen conference with disparate aims.
Trump hopes to focus the meeting on nuclear nonproliferation, urging the Russian and Chinese presidents to work with him to scale back the world’s largest nuclear stockpiles. Putin pressed for the meeting to discuss his ongoing war in Ukraine . And Xi wants to discuss neither, only embracing the idea of the summit to show the world China can help broker peace on the international stage, Chinese officials told The Times.
“That’ll be interesting,” Trump said earlier this week,  teasing the trilateral summit before the White House formally confirmed the meeting Friday.
“We’re talking a lot of things, including denuclearization,” he added, “but we’ll be talking a lot of things.”
U.S. officials have acknowledged they do not expect the meeting to result in a breakthrough on arms control. China is openly racing to build up its nuclear capacity — a nonnegotiable policy in Beijing, which sees its arsenal dwarfed by an American stockpile nearly 10 times the size.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement. I would characterize this as the entry point,” one senior Trump administration official said. “This is the beginning of hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward.”
Trump’s break from long-standing tradition in U.S.-Russia relations was real, but it should not have been entirely surprising.
The Chinese, too, threw cold water on the chances of a breakthrough, with one Chinese official telling The Times the central government saw no benefit to a pause.
“It is a matter of survival,” the official said.
The United States and Russia still command the world’s two dominant nuclear arsenals, with over 5,000 warheads each. China has an estimated 620 — but in catching up, it is developing new warheads with more sophisticated delivery systems.
Moscow, too, is modernizing its weapons, after the Trump administration allowed the last major U.S.-Russian nuclear arms treaty to expire earlier this year.
Though expectations are low for a nuclear breakthrough, Trump doesn’t want to discuss Putin’s priorities, either, the U.S. official added.
“He does not intend to talk about Ukraine in that meeting,” the official said. “China is not really part of that track, so it doesn’t really seem appropriate.”
Ukraine has grown increasingly concerned by Trump’s pressure campaign to force it into concessions to Moscow as he pushes to end the war.
The Trump administration has brought Russian and Ukrainian officials together at a working level to explore the viability of peace talks. But a long-standing U.S. policy on the war — not to negotiate about Ukraine without Ukraine — could be further compromised at a trilateral with Putin and Xi.
The only American business leader confirmed to join Trump in Asia is Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX chief who was seen as instrumental in the decision last month to restrict Ukraine’s access on the battlefield to Starlink , the satellite internet service owned by Musk.
Beijing has struck a careful balance on Ukraine, publicly issuing its respect for sovereign borders — a position popular among Chinese voices who support Kyiv — while giving Moscow diplomatic cover, an economic lifeline and technological support throughout the war.
The summit’s stark lack of substance surprised even the closest China watchers.
Their competing agendas could make the summit little more than a spectacle, yet still produce images that hark back to the famous Yalta Conference — held in Crimea, the Ukrainian peninsula currently occupied by Russia, in 1945 — where Josef Stalin, Franklin Delano Roosevelt and Winston Churchill carved up a postwar order.
The summit on Chinese soil offers Xi a powerful image to broadcast worldwide , demonstrating an emergent superpower can bring together the leaders of two historic rivals in the name of peace.
Putin gets to present himself as a global player, despite the devastation wrought on Russia’s economy and military standing after four bruising years of war.
And it allows Trump to reassert his global relevance after this month’s midterms delivered the worst electoral rebuke to a president in half a century, rivaling the backlash against President Nixon during Watergate.

articles.title_orig: Ukrainian troops say they battled through underground gas pipeline to launch attack behind Russian lines
articles.title_zh: Ukrainian troops say they battled through underground gas pipeline to launch attack behind Russian lines
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian soldiers spent weeks navigating a decommissioned, underground Soviet-era gas pipeline to sneak behind enemy lines and launch a surprise attack on Russian troops this autumn as part of an operation to prevent the invading forces from reaching the eastern city of Kupiansk, according to the Ukrainian unit involved.
The operation forced the soldiers to get past barricades laid by Russian forces — including the bodies of fallen troops —   and involved close-quarters combat inside the roughly three-foot-wide pipeline, Ukraine's military said.
"Operation Veles" was carried out by members of the Ukrainian National Guard's Khartiia Corps in the Kharkiv region within the last couple of months, according to a series of posts by the unit on social media. The unit said troops crawled and were pulled on wheeled carts some nine miles through the underground pipeline before emerging behind Russian positions.
The operation was part of a broader Ukrainian effort, more than four and a half years into Russia's full-scale invasion , to prevent the invading forces from advancing toward the front-line city of Kupiansk.
The unit's social media posts quoted soldiers saying they engaged in close combat with grenades and small arms inside the pipe, where the cramped space came with pooled freezing water and traces of natural gas lingering years after the pipeline was decommissioned. Some Ukrainian forces spent as long as a month underground during the operation, the Khartiia Corps said.
"They used electric winches to move through the pipe, and transported ammunition and equipment on small wheelbarrows," the unit said in one post. It called the conditions "extremely harsh," and noted that the troops "constantly moving on their knees caused injuries, and dirt clogged the mechanisms of their weapons and caused malfunctions."
Russian troops had laid obstacles in some sections of the pipeline, with Ukrainian soldiers saying that some of those barricades included the bodies of other Russian soldiers. The claims by the Ukrainian forces about the battle have not been independently verified by CBS News.
Russian authorities have acknowledged the operation, referring to a Ukrainian raid.
The Khartiia Corps has not confirmed any Ukrainian casualties, but at least one report on the battle, by Britain's Telegraph newspaper, mentioned Ukrainian forces recovering the body of a fallen comrade from inside an underground gas pipeline.
The pipeline offered a way for Ukrainian forces to conceal their movements in one of the most heavily monitored sectors of the nearly 1,000-mile front line that stretches from the far north to the far south of eastern Ukraine.
Both sides have sought to exploit underground infrastructure to evade increasingly sophisticated aerial surveillance in a conflict shaped by drone warfare. In September 2025, Russian forces similarly attempted to use sections of underground pipeline to move troops closer to Ukrainian positions around the northern outskirts of Kupiansk without being detected by drones.
Military analysts say operations like the underground pipeline assault highlight how the widespread use of drones in Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion, and Ukraine's defense, have transformed modern warfare. Both sides rely heavily on surveillance and attack drones to find and strike troops and hardware moving in the open.
As a result, even short movements above ground can expose soldiers to near real-time observation and attack.
While underground operations present their own dangers, including limited ventilation, restricted movement, navigational challenges and the risk of entrapment, soldiers involved in the Ukrainian mission suggested the hazards were outweighed by the dangers posed above ground, where they could have been spotted by Russian drones.
"It's damp, it's dark, it reeks. There are corpses lying around, but I felt safer there," one Khartiia Corps member, using the callsign "Sgt. Santa," was quoted as saying in a post by the unit.
The operation came ahead of what could prove a critical juncture in the war. President Trump, who campaigned on ending the war quickly, has pushed hard for Ukraine and Russia to agree to a peace deal. Kyiv and its European allies fear, however, that the White House appears to be offering Vladimir Putin and Russia too much — including the prospect of major energy deals, with no significant concessions in return,  while putting pressure on Ukraine to make major territorial concessions without any concrete security guarantees.
Ukraine says the operation in the gas pipeline helped stop Russian forces from gaining more ground near Kupiansk, a city that Ukrainian forces recaptured from Russia's invading troops in 2022.
Mariia  Kashchenko contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Social media algorithms are encouraging Americans to freak out about the tech outages
articles.title_zh: Social media algorithms are encouraging Americans to freak out about the tech outages
articles.content_orig:
By PHILLIP NIETO, US POLITICAL REPORTER
Published: 09:27 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 14:17 EST, 17 November 2026
JD Vance has told Americans they do not need a bunker or a food stockpile, days after a global email collapse, a nationwide ground stop and a banking meltdown.
‘A lot of my friends have reached out asking if they should prepare to build a bunker or stock up on food and water,’ the vice president told Fox News host Laura Ingraham on Monday night.
‘We don’t see a crisis coming down,’ Vance added, ‘but you have to be prepared for everything.’
‘We want to make sure we prevent the worst outcomes, but we’re also prepared for the worst outcomes,’ he continued.
Ingraham had asked him point blank whether Americans should be prepping for a major global catastrophe. It comes after Britain and France have told their own citizens to keep days of food and water at home.
Vance brushed off the reporting behind the question, including accounts of Pentagon bases preparing to run off the grid for 90 days, as ‘just basic good government, making sure that our military is prepared, God forbid, if there was a crisis.’
Meanwhile, Google has warned corporate America that hackers powered by artificial intelligence are running autonomous attacks across major systems.
The company's report released on Monday claims these AI hackers can constantly work around security patches, write working exploits and fire them at online servers.
Vance has told Americans they do not need a bunker or a food stockpile, days after a global email collapse, a nationwide ground stop and a banking meltdown
Google has warned corporate America that hackers powered by artificial intelligence are now running autonomous attacks across major systems
Tens of thousands of travelers were left stranded over the weekend after the FAA issued a nationwide grounding for all flights
Google drew no connection between its findings and last week’s failures, and federal officials say they have found no evidence that anyone attacked anything.
Moreover, Hackers have compromised some of the world’s most visited websites in a sweeping cyberattack targeting users’ money and credit card details.
Security researchers identified malicious code in website tools used by 178 organizations, including Zoom, CNN, the BBC, HSBC, Equifax, Salesforce, Peacock, IKEA, Fox News, NPR, the ASPCA and Invisalign.
The attack, detected Monday evening, targeted Optimizely, a service companies use to test different website layouts and features.
Microsoft’s Outlook, Teams and Copilot services collapsed on Thursday and stayed down for users in 74 countries into the weekend.
On Friday, approxiatemately 10,000 flights were disrupted after the Federal Aviation Administration halted departures across the country, the second nationwide ground stop since the September 11 attacks.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has blamed a router that contractor L3Harris Technologies installed at a remote FAA radio site in Arkansas.
It flooded a network still running on equipment built in 2001 and scheduled for replacement in 2006.
Duffy called FBI Director Kash Patel to pull agents into the investigation, the router now sits in a laboratory in Florida, and the FAA has switched off the broadcast function on all 69 of the same devices across the national airspace.
By Monday, banks had been affected by the the outages as thousands of customers at Chase, Wells Fargo, US Bank, Capital One, Truist and Bank of America reporting they could not see their balances or move cash.
United Airlines also delayed its own departures that same afternoon when pilots lost the weight and balance figures they need to leave the gate, stopping hundreds of flights.

articles.title_orig: FAA pauses installation of new routers after ground stop
articles.title_zh: FAA pauses installation of new routers after ground stop
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Aviation Administration said Tuesday it would pause the installation of new routers after problems with the technology led the agency to issue a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday.
Tens of thousands of flights were affected by the ground stop, which halted departing flights for more than four hours. It was the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that an overloaded router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies appeared to overwhelm systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the news about the pause.
The FAA and Department of Transportation have said L3Harris was working to convert the communications network from copper wires to fiber optic.
Democratic members of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation this week asked the FAA and the Department of Transportation for clarity on what went wrong.
"Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed," the senators wrote in a statement. "Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety."
The agencies have said they are working to figure out the root cause of the issue and have reiterated that there is no indication of a cyberattack or outside threat.
The senators also asked for a briefing with the FAA, L3Harris and Juniper Networks, which is making the new devices, by Monday. They asked the companies to lay out why the operational systems lacked sufficient redundancy and answer other questions about what led to the outage.
CNBC has reached out to L3Harris and Juniper Networks for comment.
Duffy on Friday called for Congress to approve $50 billion in funding for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system, more than he has previously asked for. Democratic lawmakers pushed back on the request, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress' approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years.
Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday that he thinks there will be support for air traffic control modernization, but that the allocation should be specifically for safety upgrades.
"I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded," he said. "Some of that is not safety related, but we just discussed there, and what I expressed is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization."
Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have for years angered airline executives, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions.
— CNBC's Phil LeBeau , Leslie Josephs and Justin Papp contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge has collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Moscow's war effort.
The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before" and that Russian President Vladimir Putin had been briefed on the overnight attack.
Elsewhere, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges - key crossings over the Dnipro River - had been closed after Russia hit Ukraine's capital overnight.
The Southern bridge partially reopened on Tuesday, Klitschko said.
Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.
While Kyiv has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.
The Crimean Bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and illegally annexed Ukraine's southern peninsula in 2014.
The $3.6bn (£2.7bn) piece of infrastructure is widely seen in Russia and Ukraine as Putin's personal pet project: His close tycoon friend Arkady Rotenberg built it, and then Putin personally opened it by driving a lorry over it in May 2018.
In Ukraine, the much-hated bridge is seen as one of the main symbols of Russia's continuing occupation of Ukrainian lands.
"We're drinking champagne!" Andrii, an engineer who lives in Kyiv, told the BBC.
He said the latest attack would "deal a very heavy blow to the morale of the Russians".
Some Ukrainians are concerned that Putin might now respond by carrying out even more attacks against civilian infrastructure, but Andrii said: "I don't think the Russians can make things much worse; they're already pounding us every single night with everything they've got."
The damage after the overnight attack, involving cruise missiles and drones, appeared to be far more severe than during previous strikes on the bridge, with a large arched section apparently destroyed.
Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.
Zelensky said the strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".
He said several types of Ukrainian drones as well as the country's Flamingo and Neptune cruise missiles were fired overnight during a "pivotal stage".
The Ukrainian president also said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and Russia's transport ministry later said some rail services resumed.
Ukraine's state security service SBU said its operations had "systematically suppressed enemy air defence systems" over a month, and said it showed "no Russian defence systems can guarantee the safety of illegal objects occupied by the invaders".
Meanwhile, Ukraine's military said the roadway on the bridge is "out of action", with no vehicle able to cross it, and the railway section is still standing, but with a damaged arch.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.
Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".
For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry.
Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.
In Kyiv, loud explosions were heard just before midnight on Monday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water supplies.
On Tuesday, Zelensky said four ballistic missiles had targeted the Southern Bridge, and another three had been fired on the Northern Bridge.
Some of Kyiv's above-ground metro services were also damaged in the overnight attacks, local officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.
Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River, connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.
Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the central Cherkasy region, according to local officials.
The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear, though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.
The collapse of the arched section has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia – at least until the crossing can be repaired.
However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of Ukraine's southern Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Kyiv has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.
This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.
There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait, which connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Azov. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.
Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.
In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge – particularly its enormous arch – may have blocked the shipping channel.
This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for the Russian-occupied ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdyansk.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.

articles.title_orig: A Kremlin trap? Europe sees danger in Vladimir Putin’s new demand in U.S. talks
articles.title_zh: A Kremlin trap? Europe sees danger in Vladimir Putin’s new demand in U.S. talks
articles.content_orig:
Russian attacks have killed at least three people in Ukraine, as the European Union accuses Moscow of stalling talks aimed at ending the war.
Russia carried out several attacks on Monday, including in the village of Sadove in southern Ukraine’s Kherson region, killing a man on a moped, according to Governor Oleksandr Prokudin.
Another person was killed in a Russian attack in Dnipro city in central Ukraine, according to Oleksandr Hanzha, the head of the Dnipropetrovsk region’s military administration.
Elsewhere, a 59-year-old man was killed in a Russian drone attack in the village of Bilenke in the southern region of Zaporizhia, said Mykhailo Semikin, the acting head of the region’s military administration.
Monday’s attacks come as EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs Kaja Kallas accused Russian President Vladimir Putin of making maximalist demands in a bid to extend the conflict.
After negotiations in Abu Dhabi last week, the United States encouraged Ukraine and its backers to agree to a Russian demand for a new security framework for Europe, suggesting that it might help bring peace.
But the Europeans see that as a Russian attempt to weaken NATO by obliging the military alliance to pull troops and equipment back westward, similar to the way they were deployed before the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland joined in 1999.
“In 2021, Russia’s demands were a pretext for war. In 2026, they are pretext to keep the war going,” Kallas said in a post on X.
“A ceasefire must come first. It must be the basis to start the talks about anything else. With EU Foreign Ministers, we will discuss our own demands on Moscow to reply to the maximum demands that Russia is presenting.”
Meanwhile, Ukrainian drone attacks in the Belgorod region of southwest Russia killed one person on Monday, local authorities said.
The Russian Defence Ministry said on Monday that it had intercepted 1,336 drones during overnight attacks by Ukraine.
Kyiv received $1.88bn from the European Commission on Monday to buy drones, ammunition and air ⁠defence systems. The money is part of a larger $99bn loan approved in February. Separately, the EU approved its largest-ever single payment to Ukraine, about $8.7bn.
“Thank you to [the] EU Commission and EU Council for approving the largest-ever single payment to Ukraine under the Ukraine Facility, amounting to nearly €8 billion [$8.7bn],” Zelenskyy said in a post on X.
“I thank President Von Der leyen for her personal efforts to expedite the preparation of this payment, given Ukraine’s growing budgetary needs ahead of winter and intensified Russian attacks on our energy, heating, water supply, and other critical infrastructure.”
The EU is currently pushing for a ceasefire followed by a lasting peace agreement to end the four-and-a-half-year conflict.
The bloc on Monday imposed more sanctions on Russia, targeting nearly 50 banks and financial institutions. Several businesspeople with links to the energy sector, the trade in oil, and petroleum products were also sanctioned.
Dozens of others accused of spreading pro-Russian propaganda and disinformation were also hit with travel bans and asset freezes.
Last week, two days of talks between Russian and Ukrainian officials were held in the United Arab Emirates.
The discussions were mediated by the US and led to an agreement on a prisoner exchange. However, they failed to make a breakthrough on ending the war.
