articles.title_orig: Google makes it easier to use Gemini without training AI on your data
articles.title_zh: Google makes it easier to use Gemini without training AI on your data
articles.content_orig:
Google is extending how long it keeps temporary Gemini chats and conversations made with chat history turned off to around two months, saying the change aims to improve safety and security as AI systems become more capable.
The change , which will roll out globally in the Gemini app over the coming weeks, marks a significant increase from the previous 72-hour retention period mentioned in Google’s Gemini Apps Privacy Hub, according to an archived version from November 12.
OpenAI, by comparison, says it may keep temporary chats in ChatGPT for up to 30 days, whereas Anthropic retains incognito chats in Claude for 30 days by default. However, companies may keep some data longer for legal or safety reasons, or to investigate policy violations.
Google did not answer questions about what prompted the change and whether it would affect how conversations are accessed or reviewed, instead pointing to a blog post that says chats are kept longer to respond to users, process feedback, and protect its services and users. Its updated Gemini Apps Privacy Hub also cites potential system failures as a reason for retaining chats and says temporary conversations are not used to train AI models.
The longer retention period comes as Google introduces separate settings for Gemini’s chat history and AI training. Until now, both were tied to a single “Keep Activity” setting. Users will now be able to keep their conversations in their chat history without using them to train Google’s generative AI models.
Google says both new settings will be turned off by default for users who previously disabled Keep Activity. For those who had Keep Activity turned on, their chat history will remain enabled. They can, though, decide separately whether Google can use their conversations to train AI models.

articles.title_orig: CA DMV bans Waymos from operating on state freeways after Bay Area traffic incidents
articles.title_zh: CA DMV bans Waymos from operating on state freeways after Bay Area traffic incidents
articles.content_orig:
The California Department of Motor Vehicles has ordered Waymo to stop operating its autonomous vehicles on California freeways, citing concerns that the vehicles pose an imminent public safety hazard.
The DMV's decision follows a series of incidents involving Waymo vehicles on Bay Area freeways, specifically citing two of them.
One of the incidents noted by the agency involved three Waymo vehicles that entered an active construction zone on U.S. Highway 101 near Burlingame, putting workers, equipment and other vehicles at risk. According to the DMV, similar incidents have occurred multiple times.
The other incident cited by the DMV drew additional attention after images showed a Waymo vehicle attempting to pass California Highway Patrol patrol cars conducting a traffic break on Interstate 280 earlier this month.
VIDEO: Driverless Waymo tries to bypass CHP traffic break on SF freeway
In a statement, Waymo said safety remains its top priority.
"Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations," a spokesperson told ABC7 Eyewitness News.
The DMV said concerns about Waymo vehicles on freeways are not new.
This is the second time this year Waymo has faced freeway restrictions. In May 2026 , Waymo said it was pausing freeway operations in several cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles, to improve how its vehicles respond in construction zones.
The California DMV says these new restrictions went into effect on November 11 and "will remain in place until Waymo demonstrates to the Department that it has taken effective corrective actions..."
"I see this as an opportunity to continue improving a technology," said Billy Riggs, a professor at the University of San Francisco.
Riggs said data shows autonomous vehicles remain safer than human drivers overall, but added that challenges are expected as the technology continues to develop.
MORE: Study finds lower crash rate for Waymo vehicles in San Francisco
"An automated vehicle can understand and identify all the aspects of the roadway and make really sophisticated judgments on them. But, many times, it can't understand context," Riggs said.
Earlier this year, San Francisco resident Elliot Slade said he was riding in a Waymo vehicle when it went off course and entered a construction zone. ABC7 Eyewitness News previously spoke with Slade about the incident and interviewed him again Monday.
"I used to use it all the time and now it's like ehh I'll walk, or I'll take the (bus)," Slade said.
Slade said the experience left him skeptical about using Waymo vehicles in the future. While he acknowledged that accidents can happen with any vehicle, he said he remains concerned about the potential consequences if similar incidents continue.
"You had one chance to fix it if it went viral. And if they haven't made sure it's completely safe, then I'm disappointed. Super disappointed," Slade said.

articles.title_orig: Sony defeats £2 billion UK claim over PlayStation Store pricing
articles.title_zh: Sony defeats £2 billion UK claim over PlayStation Store pricing
articles.content_orig:
Sony has defeated a major $2.6 billion UK class action lawsuit over the price of PlayStation games.
The lawsuit was brought about by Alex Neill, who is representing consumers that purchased PlayStation digital content between August 2016 and February 2026. The action accused PlayStation of having a ‘near monopoly’ on digital games and add-on content on PlayStation platforms. The case argued that Sony sets strict terms and conditions on developers, and charges a 30% commission on every purchase, which results in “excessive and unfair prices”. It claimed the prices are out of proportion to the costs.
But London’s Competition Appeal Tribunal rejected this, and said the claim failed to establish that PlayStation infringed competition law. As a result, it has dismissed the case in its entirety.
Join The Game Business Today!
The lawsuit argued that once you own a PlayStation, you are trapped within the ecosystem. The Tribunal disagreed, and ruled that Sony competes within a wider ‘systems market’ with the likes of Xbox, Nintendo and PC. It also ruled that gamers can buy physical games (at least for now).
The court said that forcing PlayStation to allow third-party stores onto the platform would be expensive, complex and could impact security. It added that under competition law, there was no legal duty for Sony to do this.
Finally, the court didn’t find pricing to be unfair. It said that Alex Neill had failed to prove Sony’s profit margins were excessive, especially as console makers sell hardware cheaply to make money back on game sales. Furthermore, there tribunal said there no evidence that rival stores would have brought pricing down.
PlayStation still faces similar class actions in Australia, Netherlands and Portugal at an earlier stage.
For more details on the Alex Neill case, you can read our run-down from earlier this year.
The Game Business is a reader-supported publication. Join us today!
Sony's digital store has always charged significantly more than physical stores, despite digital obviously having lower production costs/overheads.
Forcing Sony to allow alternate stores isn't the answer but forcing Sony to allow retailers to sell digital codes would have been a fair compromise, potentially recreating the pre-digital dynamic.
Not only would this result in positive pricing competition, it might allow the games retail scene to grow again, and help sustain nice shops/third spaces for gamers to come together rather than it all be done online.
Perhaps current competition law isn't equipped to deal with the digital age and needs to be reviewed?

articles.title_orig: Trump’s New A.I. Chip Rules Rattle Southeast Asia
articles.title_zh: Trump’s New A.I. Chip Rules Rattle Southeast Asia
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia warned its customers that new legislation on Chinese companies remotely accessing its artificial-intelligence chips could expose it and them to U.S. "legal action," sources told CNBC.
The chip giant is facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China.
Nvidia messaged chip buyers in recent months to caution that the proposed Remote Access Security Act, or RASA, would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services in the same way as physical hardware, potentially exposing both parties to legal risk, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. The people asked not to be named while discussing private communications.
It also said that, for now, it would not sell its chips to customers who rent more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies, the people said.
Separately, the Financial Times reported earlier this month that Nvidia verbally told data-center clients to direct at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese customers under future contracts.
Regulators have had limited powers to control companies' access to those chips through cloud services hosted overseas.
RASA passed the House of Representatives in January but has not yet passed the Senate. Remote access to the chips has provoked the ire of President Donald Trump 's administration, which has sought to keep the chips out of China to maintain the U.S. lead in the AI race.
CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that Chinese lab Moonshot AI sought access to Nvidia chips through data centers in Europe. The Trump administration previously singled the company out, accusing it in July of accessing the chips through centers in East Asia.
The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.
Nvidia and BIS did not respond to a request for comment.
On Sunday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia after Jensen Huang 's shock departure as CEO, amid reports of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. authorities reportedly suspect of spying for China.
Bessent suggested other Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with export controls.
"I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent told Fox News.
In an August securities filing , Nvidia said it sought to "strictly comply with all applicable export control regulators" but did not have "physical control of our products after sale" and relied on its customers' and partners' compliance programs.
Huang has been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

articles.title_orig: Deutsche Bank Leak Exposes Epstein Payments—Democrats Could Hold It And Other Banks Accountable
articles.title_zh: Deutsche Bank Leak Exposes Epstein Payments—Democrats Could Hold It And Other Banks Accountable
articles.content_orig:
Deutsche Bank shares fell sharply in early trading on Tuesday after whistleblowers leaked about 15 million files from the German lender, with media reports revealing alleged historic failures across its risk management and financial crime controls.
These include suspicious payments linked to late financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and accidental leaks of President Donald Trump 's tax statements.
The leaks contain board minutes, emails, internal investigations and other material that point to systemic failures across the Frankfurt-listed lender's business functions stretching back two decades.
Shares in Deutsche Bank were 4.7% lower by 9:20 a.m. E.T., having fallen more than 6% in early trade in Frankfurt.
Deutsche Bank processed $582 million in suspicious payments linked to Jeffrey Epstein, far more than previously known, the FT reported . Suspicious payments are not, by themselves, proof that every transaction was criminal.
The German lender also mistakenly leaked details of U.S. President Donald Trump's taxes in March 2017, during his first term in office, the FT said. The blunder — described by CEO Christian Sewing, who was then Deutsche's private banking head, as "an awful mistake" — was kept secret from the White House.
The wide-ranging investigation — which was led by a consortium of more than 200 journalists worldwide including the FT, Der Spiegel and Le Monde — also said Deutsche Bank had failed to offboard around 28,000 problematic investment bank clients who had been identified for removal by early 2018.
It also alleges that the bank concealed information around cost targets in 2021, when external monitors in New York reportedly warned that Deutsche's risk appetite was running ahead of controls.
The files also contain details of the bank's relationships with oligarchs and transactions that the investigation links to Russian money-laundering concerns. It was these ties that motivated whistleblowers to send the information to Indian journalist Josy Joseph and South African journalist Khadija Sharife.
The reports once again put Deutsche Bank's risk management practices and controls under the spotlight following years of regulatory scrutiny.
The bank — which has been raided multiple times by German officials this year — has, since 2012, paid out some 18.6 billion euros ($20.5 billion) in settlements over alleged market manipulation, money laundering, mis-selling and misrepresentation, among other things, the FT said.
In a statement, Deutsche Bank said the issues detailed in Tuesday's media reports go back many years.
"Where relevant, we reviewed these matters at the time and worked closely with regulators," the lender said.
The bank said it has undergone a "fundamental transformation" under CEO Christian Sewing, pointing to 7 billion euros of investment in its risk controls between 2019 and 2025.
"Deutsche Bank is a different bank today and remains focused on executing its strategy which has proven successful, as evidenced by record profits in 2025 as well as in recent quarters."
CNBC has reached out to BaFin, Germany's financial regulator, for comment.

articles.content_orig:

As gamers anxiously await this week’s release of Grand Theft Auto VI , Fox News hosts are already starting the culture wars over the crime-fueled video game series.
Fox & Friends Weekend hosts Rachel Campos-Duffy, Charles Hurt and Griff Jenkins recently looked at a preview of the new game , featuring characters Jason Duval, an Army veteran working for local drug runners, and Lucia Caminos, who was previously jailed after fighting for her family.
“I’m gonna push back a little,” Campos-Duffy, wife of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy , said. “I’m not thinking that this is a good thing for our culture.”
Jenkins then suggested Campos-Duffy could play as Luicia, prompting her to ask, “Is she the hooker?”
“No, she’s a partner-in-crime,” Jenkins said. Campos-Duffy then laughed it off. “You can maybe play and get her to go straight,” Jenkins added.
Conservatives and liberals have long fought over cultural beliefs, typically when it comes to civil rights, including diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives and LGBTQ+ issues.
Fox News is known to promote the conservative view, railing against DEI and trans rights. And now, the network is coming after your favorite video game.
In Grand Theft Auto VI , set to be released at midnight on Thursday, Jason and Lucia will find themselves in the middle of a criminal conspiracy in the fictional state of Leonida, where they will need to rely on each other to make it out alive.
Grand Theft Auto , or GTA for short, is one of the most popular gaming franchises of the century. GTA fans have been waiting more than a decade for a new game in the series, making Thursday’s release even more exciting for them.
Roughly 15 million copies of Ground Theft Auto VI have been preordered, CNN Business reported, citing Sensor Tower data.
Strauss Zelnick, the CEO of GTA’s publisher, Take-Two Interactive, told Variety that presales of the new game are “running far in excess of our expectations.”
Violent games like GTA , Call of Duty and Mortal Kombat have faced scrutiny over the years for potentially leading to bad behavior in players, such as aggression.
But a study published in Molecular Psychiatry in 2018 found no changes in behavior between participants who played Grand Theft Auto V , the non-violent video game The Sims 3 and those who played no game at all.

articles.title_orig: Take-Two’s Firaxis, Maker of ‘Civilization,’ Cuts a Third of Its Staff
articles.title_zh: Take-Two’s Firaxis, Maker of ‘Civilization,’ Cuts a Third of Its Staff
articles.content_orig:
The Civilization and XCOM developer is shrinking as a new XCOM game has missed a development milestone, according to Bloomberg
Take-Two Interactive $TTWO 's Firaxis Games cut roughly 60 jobs on Tuesday, about one-third of the studio's workforce, according to Bloomberg .
A spokesperson from 2K Games, the Take-Two imprint that oversees Firaxis, verified that Heather Hazen, who heads the studio, is departing, according to Bloomberg. The Maryland-based studio makes the Civilization and XCOM franchises.
"Firaxis is restructuring and recentering around the studio's core strength — designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years," the spokesperson said in a statement, according to Bloomberg. "As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis."
The spokesperson described Hazen’s exit as a planned handover, according to Game Developer . “With the studio entering this reset, she feels this is the right, deliberate moment to hand over the reins to ensure the next studio leader has full ownership of this new era from the start,” the spokesperson said, according to Game Developer.
Firaxis has been working on a new XCOM title that ran into development problems and fell short of an important milestone this summer, according to Bloomberg. Bloomberg, citing unnamed people, said work on the game will go on, though the cuts could bring major changes to it.
“Civilization VII,” the studio’s latest title, came out last year to a lukewarm response and has been patched repeatedly since, according to Bloomberg. The game holds a 51% positive user rating on Steam, according to Kotaku .
The layoffs land just two days prior to “Grand Theft Auto VI” hitting the market, according to Bloomberg. Rockstar, a separate Take-Two label, develops and publishes that game.

articles.title_orig: 6-year-old girl dies in gene-editing trial, leading to scientist's firing, Chinese state media reports
articles.title_zh: 6-year-old girl dies in gene-editing trial, leading to scientist's firing, Chinese state media reports
articles.content_orig:
A Chinese scientist who concealed the death of a 6-year-old girl in a gene-editing trial has been fired following a government probe, according to state media.
The girl died last year after receiving experimental gene therapy to correct a non-life-threatening condition — which was not disclosed in published research, an investigation found in July.
Neuroscientist Zilong Qiu, the trial's lead researcher, had made no mention of the girl in a paper published in the prestigious journal Nature, according to the joint investigation by Science and Retraction Watch .
"According to official documents and accounts provided by the girl's parents, the hospital had allowed Qiu's experimental treatment to proceed under a regulatory provision that does not require approval from national regulators," Science reported in July. "After the child's death, the hospital paid a modest fine to a local health authority but Qiu was not publicly sanctioned."
Qiu was dismissed as deputy director of the Songjiang Research Institute affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University, state broadcaster CCTV said Friday, citing a statement from Shanghai authorities.
The reported statement included only Qiu's surname, but referenced the Nature study published on Feb. 18.
Qiu was given a five-year suspension from participating in scientific projects and recorded in a database for "serious breaches of research integrity," the report said.
Another researcher on Qiu's team was fired and handed a five-year suspension, while several others with ties to the hospital where the trial took place were also punished.
The child who died had a rare neurodevelopmental condition called Snijders Blok-Campeau syndrome, according to the report.
The hospital's ethics committee had approved a gene-editing trial to treat the disorder in January 2025, the report said.
The committee terminated the study after the girl died in March due to complications from gene therapy.
Shanghai authorities found that Qiu's team failed to properly inform the hospital of possible safety issues from earlier tests on primates, according to the report.
AFP has reached out to Qiu for comment.
The July investigation by Science and Retraction Watch found that the girl's parents, who paid more than $800,000 to fund the experiment, were not adequately informed about the risks.
"Learning the reality of these missing safeguards has fundamentally changed how we now view the entire project," the girl's father, told Science . "We did not realize how unusual and dangerous many of the arrangements were."
The scandal is a blow to China's ambitions to rival the United States as a biotech power following the 2018 scandal around He Jiankui , a biophysicist who secretly produced gene-edited babies. He was later sentenced to three years in prison.

articles.title_orig: Kalshi takes down controversial Trump 'mention' markets at CFTC's request
articles.title_zh: Kalshi takes down controversial Trump 'mention' markets at CFTC's request
articles.content_orig:
Prediction market platform Kalshi quietly paused trading in a handful of "mention" contracts tied to President Donald Trump at the end of last week at the request of the CFTC, the company confirmed on Tuesday.
Mention markets are made up of contracts that ask traders what specific words will be used in a speech, a corporate earnings call or during a television broadcast.  Earlier this year, a White House teleprompter operator used inside information to place trades in mention markets related to the president's comments.
Markets paused include those asking traders what nicknames Trump will say before 2027, what the president will say in November and what countries and companies Trump will say before the end of the month.
The move comes after the Commodity Futures Trading Commission , the federal agency overseeing prediction markets, said in a letter to exchanges in September that mentions contracts have a greater manipulation risk.
A spokesperson for the agency told CNBC that the commission has placed holds on the certification of some of Kalshi's proposed mention markets. The spokesperson cited a Kalshi contract on hold that asked what key words would Trump say before a certain date. The contract was originally self-certified by Kalshi in February 2025.
"The CFTC stayed the certification of these contracts because they may be susceptible to manipulation, which is consistent with the staff advisory the CFTC put out two months ago," said Brooke Nethercott, the agency's spokesperson.
In a statement, Kalshi spokesperson Dani Lever said Kalshi is complying with the order.
In August, reports emerged that the CFTC was conducting an internal review into mention markets. The agency also requested that Kalshi, which is the only U.S.-regulated exchange that features the contract type, take down its sports-related mention markets in response to the inquiry. Kalshi complied.
A Trump-related mention market drew scrutiny in July after it was revealed a White House teleprompter operator placed trades on markets related to the president's comments. In a settlement with the operator, the CFTC ordered a three-year trading ban on the individual and a penalty amounting to over $172,000 .
Kalshi has defended mentions markets even as the CFTC has become increasingly skeptical of them, saying that the individual words of prominent people often cause billions of dollars of movement across financial markets.
In addition to scrutiny regarding mention markets, the company is also facing a probe from the CFTC about its communications about new products with the agency, though a spokesperson for the company told CNBC that it was working to resolve the issues.
As of Tuesday morning, a mention market asking what Vice President JD Vance would say during the New York Times DealBook Summit event on Wednesday is still active.
Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

articles.title_orig: US authorities interviewed Alice Huang in probe over possible diversion of chips
articles.title_zh: US authorities interviewed Alice Huang in probe over possible diversion of chips
articles.content_orig:
The Justice and Commerce Departments announced late Monday that they were pursuing a criminal investigation of Megaspeed, a Singapore company once led by a woman whom U.S. officials believe worked as a Chinese intelligence asset while having an affair with Nvidia’s chief executive.
The announcement appeared to be an effort to counter criticism that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was slow to investigate Megaspeed. It has become the most prominent example of companies that American authorities believe are skirting export rules on the powerful artificial intelligence chips made by Nvidia, the world’s leading manufacturer.
Nvidia exports have exposed a rift in the Trump administration between officials who believe American A.I. technology needs to be kept out of China for national security reasons and others who want a more hands-off approach to export controls.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a TV interview on Friday that his department had been pushing for months to add Megaspeed to a trade blacklist, but that the Commerce Department “holds the pen.”
“You will have to ask them about their internal processes,” he said.
That the Justice Department was included in the Monday night announcement appeared to add heft to the investigation’s importance and signaled to critics that administration officials did not intend to ignore the issue.
Megaspeed was created and led for a time by Alice Huang, who U.S. officials say was an asset for Chinese intelligence. The New York Times reported last year that she and Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, had a close relationship, and last week Mr. Huang admitted that he had been unfaithful to his wife with Ms. Huang.

Russia's growing dependence on China is reshaping one of the world's most important geopolitical relationships. Since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the resulting Western sanctions, Russia has relied heavily on Beijing for trade, technology and critical imports. articles.title_orig: Trump talks Nvidia, rare earths as he attends Quad and Asean meetings in Manila
articles.title_zh: Trump talks Nvidia, rare earths as he attends Quad and Asean meetings in Manila
articles.content_orig:
David E. Sanger and Katie Rogers
President Trump landed in Manila on Tuesday to begin a 48-hour Asia trip in which he will meet with Xi Jinping of China and other world leaders, with an unpredictable agenda that could include the future of American tariffs, nuclear arms control, the war in Ukraine and U.S. restrictions on advanced A.I. chips.
Mr. Trump was scheduled to meet with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines and attend a gathering of Southeast Asian leaders. After less than 24 hours in Manila, he will head to the APEC economic summit in Shenzhen, China, where he was expected to meet with Mr. Xi and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.
The brief itinerary appears to reflect Mr. Trump’s preferences. He dislikes big summits where he often is not the sole subject of attention. And he enjoys meeting with leaders of powerful nations — especially Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin, two authoritarian leaders he often talks about in admiring terms.
Mr. Trump will be meeting Mr. Xi for the third time this year, and a three-way meeting between China, Russia and the United States would be the first of its kind.
On Tuesday, Mr. Trump caught the end of a dayslong meeting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or ASEAN, after issuing tariffs on countries across the region, even allies. Those moves added to a sentiment in Asia that the United States was not a reliable partner but rather one that treasured its commercial interests over its security interests. The only event of substance on the president’s schedule on Tuesday — signing what he had called a “ trade deal ” with Thailand — did not happen because Mr. Trump said it was still being finalized.
Mr. Trump met with leaders from the so-called Quad — the United States, India, Japan and Australia — soon after his arrival. All three partners are smarting from high energy prices triggered by the Iran war, a conflict Mr. Trump never discussed with them before launching it in late February.
In Shenzhen — the heart of China’s robotics and artificial intelligence industries — Mr. Trump will pursue détente with Mr. Xi. He needs to extend a soon-expiring trade truce that limited tariffs on Chinese goods entering the United States in return for a Chinese commitment not to cut off rare earths and magnets.
Then comes the main event: the meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin. Referring to the trilateral meeting, Mr. Trump told reporters before leaving Washington: “We are going to be talking about denuclearization, a tough subject because it is very hard for any of us to say we’ll get rid of our nukes.” Chinese officials have made clear they are not interested in nuclear talks until their arsenal is roughly the size of the American one.
Mr. Trump also said, “We will talk about Iran a little,” insisting the situation was in “very good shape.” Analysts say it is unlikely that the meeting will make any progress on Iran, with Russia happy to see energy prices elevated since the war began, and China eager to see them rapidly decline.
Here’s what else we’re covering:
Protests: Thousands of demonstrators assembled in downtown Manila on Tuesday in opposition to Mr. Trump’s visit and to a U.S.-led initiative called Pax Silica, which aims to unite partners around A.I. supply chains independent of China. Read more ›
North Korea: Mr. Putin could meet with Kim Jong-un if the North Korean leader also travels to China for the APEC summit, Russian state news agencies reported, citing the Kremlin’s spokesman. It was not clear whether Mr. Kim would attend the summit.
Ukraine: Mr. Trump also said he would talk about Ukraine, on which Mr. Putin’s aides are engaging in talks with the U.S. and Ukrainian officials, but also renewing demands that NATO pull back its troops to where they were before the alliance expanded toward Russia.
President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia could meet with Kim Jong-un if the North Korean leader travels to China for the APEC summit this week, the Kremlin said, reflecting the deepening of ties between their countries in recent years.
Asked about the possibility of a meeting, Dmitri S. Peskov, the Kremlin spokesman, said on Monday that it would “of course” happen if Mr. Kim went to Shenzhen, the Chinese economic hub and host city, according to Russian state news agencies. North Korea has not confirmed whether Mr. Kim plans to attend the summit.
Mr. Putin and Mr. Kim have publicly met three times since 2022, and North Korea has been a key supporter of Russia’s military actions in Ukraine.
As the war in Ukraine nears its fifth anniversary, with no end in sight, the Kremlin is expected to use Mr. Putin’s many meetings at the APEC summit to showcase how Russia is regarded as one of the major international powers alongside the United States and China.
A visit by Mr. Kim would be a rare foray outside North Korea for the leader, and it would further raise the prospect that he could meet with President Trump in China. On the first day of his 48-hour trip to Asia, Mr. Trump told reporters that Mr. Kim “would like” to come to the APEC summit. The president has repeatedly said he would like to meet with Mr. Kim again.
On Wednesday, Mr. Putin is scheduled to meet with Xi Jinping, China’s leader. On Thursday, he is set to take part in a trilateral summit with Mr. Xi and Mr. Trump, the first meeting of its kind. The Kremlin said on Monday that it was working to arrange a bilateral meeting between Mr. Putin and Mr. Trump.
Before his departure for China, Mr. Putin met on Monday in the Kremlin with Jo Yong-won, a secretary of North Korea’s ruling Workers’ Party. During the meeting, Mr. Putin said that North Korea’s help in driving Ukrainian forces from the Kursk region of Russia last year “marked a new chapter in the history of military cooperation between our countries.”
Moscow planned to unveil a monument in Kursk by the end of the year to honor the North Korean troops, Mr. Putin said.
During the final meeting of the day, with ASEAN leaders, President Trump told President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines: “I don’t want to date myself, but I knew your parents very well. They were great. I believe in genetics. They did a good job. You have very good genetics, I can tell you that.”
It was not the first time Mr. Trump has praised the family of Mr. Marcos , who is the son of the dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos, who ruled the Philippines for 20 years, imposed martial law and was ousted in 1986.
The only event of substance on President Trump’s schedule today, the signing of a trade deal between the United States and Thailand, did not happen because it was still being finalized. Trump told reporters that “Thailand will eliminate all tariffs on U.S. imports” and that the United States would provide tariff relief, but the two sides signed only a memorandum about the agreement. The president said the deal would be done in the coming weeks.
During an address to Quad leaders, President Trump called Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India, which is a member of the group, “a great leader and a friend of mine, highly respected by everybody all over the world.” The president also praised Modi as he stood with other leaders and took a few questions, calling him a “very tough man.”
India and the United States are navigating a rocky patch in their relationship, largely tied to trade and India’s purchases of Russian oil. Although Modi and Trump signed an interim framework for a trade deal in February, talks have dragged on, frustrating both parties.
The Nvidia turmoil and its implications for the U.S.-China relationship is a backdrop to President Trump’s visit. On Tuesday, shares of technology companies in Asia tumbled after the Trump administration announced rules to restrict overseas access to advanced A.I. chips like those sold by Nvidia. In Hong Kong trading, Alibaba fell 5 percent, while Tencent’s stock dropped nearly 4 percent. The Chinese A.I. firms MiniMax Group fell 7 percent, and Z.AI Co. declined 5 percent.

articles.title_orig: Customers report outages at Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo
articles.title_zh: Customers report outages at Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo
articles.content_orig:
Customers at major US banks , including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, are reporting trouble accessing some services
Chase Bank says a software bug has potentially caused ripple effects for other banks
Chase, a subsidiary of JP Morgan Chase, says it is dealing with a "technical issue" that it is working to quickly resolve
"Some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds," the bank says
Another institution, US Bank, says its systems aren't directly affected but clients using the Zelle platform to make transactions to other banks may experience delays
Zelle says its service is "operating as it should" and issues at other banks may be affecting payments
Edited by Kathryn Armstrong
Rebecka Pieder US reporter
System issues affecting some of the US's biggest banks left customers looking for answers on Monday.
They began reporting issues on the tracking website Downdetector around noon today eastern time (17:00 GMT) as those trying to access online services for banks including Chase Bank, Wells Fargo and US Bank were met with error messages, as were users of the digital payment platform Zelle.
Yet, many banks and Zelle said their services were operating normally.
In a statement on X , Chase Bank eventually provided some insight. It says a software bug in on-premise hardware systems could have been affecting other banks and that it is working diligently to resolve what it describes as a "temporary" issue.
While some people are still reporting issues on Downdetector, the number has now dropped considerably.
We are pausing our live coverage now but you can read more about the issues here.
Katy Bailes Technology journalist
Kris Beevers, CEO and co-founder of the network and infrastructure management company NetBox Labs, tells the BBC that people are right in wondering if thereâs a connection between these outages, but itâs not what they expect.
"There is no conspiracy here. There is something more ordinary, and more important to understand: the infrastructure that runs the world is changing faster than ever, and change is risk," he says.
"What weâre seeing is a much higher rate of change in the infrastructure that runs the world. Much of it is 30 to 40 years old, with decades of technical debt, and itâs now being asked to change very quickly."
He says air travel is a good example, with legacy systems hitting their limits against the demands of modern operations.
Beevers adds that AI is also part of the story as itâs putting more strain on these legacy networks, as well as creating real urgency around security.
"When vulnerabilities are discovered and exploited in a matter of hours, teams canât take months to patch. Every patch is a change to the network, so teams are moving faster than they ever have, and that pace isnât going to slow down."
He notes that teams behind these networks at airlines, banking, energy, and retail are essentially doing heart surgery on a global scale to get these networks back up and running quickly.
"Itâs worth noting that these networks have 99.99% reliability, and we only hear about them when thereâs a problem," he adds.
"I expect weâll see more meaningful outages in the infrastructure that essential parts of society depend on in coming months as the invisible infrastructure that our world depends on becomes more strained and visible.â
Lily Jamali North America Technology Correspondent
First, it was email. Then airlines. And today, some US banking systems have been affected by the blanket term âtechnical issues".
This vague phrase seems aimed at making things seem less bad. Donât worry! Itâs not rogue AI or some deeply embedded cybersecurity flaw. But understandable answers seem increasingly out of reach as these incidents take place with more frequency.
Three big outages in a week is a lot. Tech systems that govern so much of our lives feel more and more like a black box from the outside.
Then there is United Airlines, which has also been dealing with its own tech issues on Monday.
Cybersecurity experts say there is no evidence connecting the Microsoft, airline and banking disruptions over the last five days. But they say it's natural to feel jarred by the barrage of incidents.
"What this week really underscores is how tightly coupled, and fragile, our core digital infrastructure is, where a single software bug or router failure can cascade nationwide," says Sherrod DeGrippo, Vice President of Threat Intelligence for Palo Alto Networks Unit 42.
There has been a notable decrease in the number of customers reporting issues with their banks on the monitoring website Downdector since earlier on Monday but problems appear to be continuing for some.
Chase - More than 1,300 people are still reporting issues. That number was almost 5,000 earlier
Bank of America - There are still some 700 issues being reported, down from a high of over 2,100
US Bank - More than 450 outages are continuing, down from more than 1,050
Wells Fargo - Almost 400 outages are still being reported, down from more than 1,050
As Chase Bank says it is dealing with a temporary issue related to a software bug, United Airlines is also dealing with its own tech woes.
The airline says in a statement to the BBC's US partner CBS News that it is dealing with a "widespread system outage" that is affecting departing flights. Flights in progress have not been affected.
"Our teams are working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible," United adds.
It comes just days after US aviation authorities issued a nationwide ground stop of all flights over a technical failure that affected air traffic control operations.
Archie Mitchell Business reporter
Chase Bank's statement about what it believes is the cause of the issue brings clarity to the situation after fingers were pointed when reports of outages first started emerging today.
The bank said it faced a software bug which had disrupted its own services and could have had a knock-on effect on other financial providers.
Earlier, some had blamed money transfer service Zelle, with US Bank saying that while its own systems were not impacted, customers trying to send or receive Zelle payments from others may be disrupted.
A Zelle spokesman said its service is "operating as it should".
Meanwhile, the number of reported outages have dropped significantly, according to the Downdetector website, including for Chase Bank.
Monday's issues could potentially affect millions of users, as Chase Bank is the biggest bank in the US.
It serves over 86 million customers at 5,000 branches across the country, as well as 7.4 million small businesses, according to the company's website.
As we've been reporting, Chase Bank says that technical issues have potentially had knock-on effects to other banks that have been involved in transactions but that the problem is not systemic.
Thousands of people have been reporting issues accessing banking services at major US banks including Bank of America, JP Morgan Chase, and Wells Fargo, according to Downdetector, which tracks service outages based on user reports.
In a statement on X, Chase Bank says a software bug has potentially caused ripple effects for other banks.
"JP Morgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems â there is no evidence this is cyber-related.  It is taking longer than usual to service some customers.
"Where we were party to a transaction involving other banks, those banks may have been impacted, but this is not a systemic issue," the statement adds.
Chase Bank says customers still have access to their accounts and funds, and that they are working diligently to resolve the issue.
The internet monitoring site Downdetector shows a spike in problems reported by PNC and Capital One customers since early Monday afternoon.
A spokesperson for PNC told the BBC they have not been "directly impacted" by the technic

articles.title_orig: Christmas Island Is Suddenly Awash in Red
articles.title_zh: Christmas Island Is Suddenly Awash in Red
articles.content_orig: Roughly 100 million Red Crabs are currently in the middle of their famous annual migration across Australia's Christmas Island National Park, creating a mesmerizing "ruby red rush hour" that has captivated tourists. According to Parks Australia officials, the massive crustaceans make their incredible trek from the dense forest to the coast to breed by the sea immediately following the first rainfall of the wet season. The event is such a massive draw for visitors—and so perilous for the millions of "creepy commuters"—that park officials proactively close roads and construct special crab bridges to help keep the animals safe during their journey.

articles.title_orig: How new US chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China
articles.title_zh: How new US chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China
articles.content_orig:
As US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors.
On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of  data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.
The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.
South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market.
But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China.
This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress , a US-based think-tank.
China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests".
This is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips.
One of those is Singaporean data centre firm Megaspeed, whose former director Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese spy. Calls for tighter export controls have grown after Nvidia's Jensen Huang admited to an affair with her and resigned as CEO .
Megaspeed, the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia, is accused of illegally smuggling chips to Chinese companies after purchasing them for use in data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
The company has denied these allegations, defended its business as "legitimate and lawful", and said it has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". It also said Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director in late 2023 and left the firm last year.
The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, however, has said Brazil and the four South East Asian nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips that Washington wants to keep out of China's hands.
The new measures are aimed at ensuring sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the bureau added. Licences will be issued on a "case-by-case basis", it said.
Countries like Malaysia and Thailand whose data centre roll out has been heavily driven by Chinese buyers could be hit hardest, says international trade expert Naoise McDonagh from Australia's Edith Cowan University.
But the new rules are unlikely to derail the data centre boom as a whole, says Reema Bhattacharya from advisory firm Verisk Maplecroft, adding that investment backed by major tech firms and clearly identifiable customers should "remain relatively resilient".
Singapore was an early adopter of data centres but when it began limiting new construction, investment flowed to neighbours Malaysia and Thailand. Johor in Malaysia and Batam in Indonesia have also approved billions of dollars worth of data centres to catch the spillover demand.
These countries have been offering incentives such as cheaper land to attract foreign investment, including from Chinese tech giants Alibaba and Tencent.
But now, the region could find it harder to get hold of advanced chips.
The BBC has contacted Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand for comment.
Singapore said it is "engaging relevant US authorities" to understand the new rules better, and is "exploring how to facilitate trusted access" for local firms.
A spokesperson for Brazil's Ministry of Development, Industry, Trade and Services said it is aware of the US announcement and it "is closely monitoring any potential developments regarding this measure".
Malaysia previously said it welcomes data centre investment but "will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls".
The new rules also come just ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week.
Beijing has made self-sufficiency in tech a national priority and needs the best chips to build powerful AI models.
Chinese firms DeepSeek and MoonShot have come close to US rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI. So much so that The Institute for Progress estimates top US AI models lead the best Chinese platforms by only about six and half months.
"This is despite US AI companies having significantly better compute access and financing," it said.
Still, China needs advanced US chips to ensure its best AI models are competitive, experts tell the BBC.
The new restrictions on South East Asia and Brazil have taken away "one of the more practical routes Chinese AI developers had to accessing frontier computing power," Bhattacharya said.
But tighter restrictions could also push Chinese firms towards domestic semiconductors and further drive advancement at home.
That has been a longstanding dilemma for Washington, McDonagh said: whether to keep selling chips to China to retain its reliance on the US, or restrict access and risk further spurring Chinese innovation.

articles.title_orig: Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it
articles.title_zh: Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it
articles.content_orig:
Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Over five days, Grok bots installed on two separate employee laptops made 31 requests to access data stored in employee calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts. The bots performed the actions even though the employees had never ordered them and continued doing them even after employees instructed them to stop. The bots also denied having taken the actions at all.
The behavior was reported Tuesday by NewCore, the maker of a managed gateway product that acts as an intermediary between AI agents and the tools and accounts they are assigned to work with. In some cases, the unapproved access attempts occurred while the laptop with Grok Bot installed had its lid shut, or late at night while the employee was sleeping. None of the unprompted actions were recorded in Grok logs. Without the gateway logs, the employees would have had no idea they occurred. And of course, without the gateway, the unapproved accesses would have succeeded—again without the end user’s knowledge.
Once the employees learned that Grok Bot had tried to check in with accounts without prompting, one of them instructed the agent, four separate times, to stop taking any actions on its own. The agent’s reply was: “I won’t set that up, and I’ll stop offering recurring check-ins.” Despite acknowledging the explicit instructions, the Grok Bot made more unapproved access attempts. When one of the employees asked the bot if it made any accesses, it checked twice and then outputted: “Overnight into Friday morning I was idle.”
The NewCore employees sent the gateway logs to Grok Bot support personnel and asked what was causing the bots to access accounts without prompting or approval. The support team’s reply indicated the behavior was by design and intended to allow the bots to proactively take actions on behalf of users. In other words, the unrequested and unlogged access attempts were a feature designed to make Grok Bot more useful by periodically checking in and finding tasks to perform before a user even asks. The proactive check-in is a feature of Cursor, the AI coding service SpaceXSI recently acquired.
“There is no bug to patch, which is exactly why this is worse than a bug,” Ido Hoorvitch, a NewCore security researcher, wrote in an email. “A vulnerability gets fixed. This is the product working as designed: an agent that holds your credentials, acts under your identity while you sleep, ignores the one refusal you can give it, and then tells you it did nothing.”
Hoorvitch said that Grok Bot provides minimal notification of the automatic “turns,” or the cycles that occur when an agent receives instructions or context, decides what to do, and calls whatever tools it chooses. The notice comes during onboarding when the bot says it keeps working while the user is away from the computer and connects to apps and uses them the way the user does.
“It reads like a welcome message and scrolls off the screen in under a minute,” Hoorvitch said. “Nobody is asked to consent to it. Nothing says the platform will start turns with no message from you, or that those turns will use your connectors.”
The researcher said that Grok Bot documentation notes that a primary bot checks in on its own, and a changelog mentions brief background wakes, but there is no mention that the check-ins “reach into your connected apps.” Further, once a check-in runs, there is no mention of it in the chat interface or in the chat history, and as already noted, prompts to stop check-ins don’t work. Hoorvitch said the bot “always asks before making changes,” but that applies only to events in which data or changes are written to an app.
NewCore contacted Grok Bot support on November 4. At the time, users had no way to turn off the automatic check-ins. Then, eight days later, Hoorvitch said, the Cursor dashboard, the administrative console behind Grok Bot, received an update. Under bot capabilities, a new toggle called proactive messages appeared. By default, it’s set to on. When a team admin sets it to off, bots no longer run check-ins on their own.
SpaceXSI representatives didn’t answer questions sent by email.

articles.title_orig: Lisa Cook lawyer signals Fed gov won't attend Trump committee's hearing
articles.title_zh: Lisa Cook lawyer signals Fed gov won't attend Trump committee's hearing
articles.content_orig:
Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook 's attorney on Tuesday gave the strongest signal yet that his client will not attend a hearing at the White House with a "committee of inquiry" investigating mortgage fraud allegations against Cook.
The committee established last month by President Donald Trump , who has previously tried to remove Cook from the central bank's board, is pretextual and poses a threat to the Fed, attorney Abbe Lowell wrote in a letter to presidential counsel Will Scharf.
"Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution's unique status and independence," Lowell wrote in the letter, which is dated Monday and was made public Tuesday.
The latest correspondence came nearly two weeks after the White House committee delayed its proposed hearing with Cook to Dec. 14 from Nov. 5. Lowell said that any hearing with Cook could not take place until at least December because of conflicts with her Fed duties.
While Lowell had raised strong concerns from the outset about the legitimacy of the committee, he initially said Cook "welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name."
But he has continued to cast doubts on both the committee's purpose and its composition of three executive branch officials, including National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett .
Lowell's tone sounded more hostile than ever in this week's letter, the first known to be sent by either party in the matter since the Republican Party's devastating losses in the midterm elections on Nov. 3.
He accused Scharf and the committee of seeking "only to manufacture 'cause' for a predetermined removal outcome."
Lowell highlighted two top concerns. First, he asserted that Hassett "is not competent to serve on any factfinding committee" because his prior comments about Cook "demonstrate that he has prejudged the issue."
Second, Lowell called it "fundamentally unfair" that the committee is demanding Cook hand over documents "immediately," while pledging to provide the governor with its own records just seven days before the hearing.
"Your and the Committee's failure to address these legitimate issues, over multiple weeks of back-and-forth correspondence, reinforces my prior observation: President Trump's decision to fire Governor Cook has already been made," Lowell wrote.
"Consequently, this Committee process appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook or to unreasonably manufacture a supposed 'adverse inference' if she does not participate in a process that does not comport with the requirements of a fair hearing," the lawyer wrote.
Lowell told Scharf that Cook would still be prepared to appear for a hearing if the White House "implements fair procedures." But the "ultimatums" Scharf gave in his last reply in early November "do not provide a productive path forward to enabling that participation," Lowell wrote.
The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Lowell's letter.
Trump, who frequently urges the Fed to lower interest rates, has long sought to fire Cook, an appointee of former President Joe Biden .
Cook, the first Black woman to serve on the Fed's Board of Governors, last voted to cut rates in December 2025, siding with the majority. The Fed unanimously voted to raise rates after its meeting in September.
Trump officials sent a criminal referral last year alleging Cook may have committed mortgage fraud by falsely claiming different properties as her primary residence in order to get more favorable terms. Cook adamantly denied wrongdoing, and, after Trump tried to fire her in August 2025, filed a lawsuit to block her removal.
The Supreme Court in June prevented Trump from firing Cook, but gave him a path to try again if additional legal steps were taken. In August, the White House told Cook it was reviving its efforts to fire her on mortgage-related grounds. In October, Trump signed a presidential memo establishing the committee of inquiry to investigate allegations that Cook lied on records related to "one or more mortgage instruments."

articles.title_orig: Dead racehorse found in dumpster days after running in prestigious race: "Distressing and completely unacceptable"
articles.title_zh: Dead racehorse found in dumpster days after running in prestigious race: "Distressing and completely unacceptable"
articles.content_orig:
The dead body of Melbourne Cup horse So You Are was found in a waste facility in Sydney less than two weeks after competing in the most prestigious event in Australian horse racing.
The Sydney Morning Herald newspaper reported Tuesday that racing stewards were investigating after a construction worker saw a dead horse in a dumpster at a licensed waste center and posted a video on Facebook.
Trainer Bjorn Baker had released a statement Monday saying So You Are died following a severe bout of colic. The 5-year-old gelding was rushed to a specialist equine hospital for emergency veterinary treatment but couldn't be saved.
Baker posted an update Tuesday after discovering So You Are hadn't been properly buried.
"Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are's remains," Baker said in a statement. "He was a much-loved horse, and he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death."
"I understand the specialist hospital facility REC Equine Specialists are investigating the circumstances, and I expect a full explanation of what occurred," he added. "My thoughts remain with the Ramsey family [owners], and with all my staff, for whom this has compounded an already devastating loss."
So You Are placed eighth in the Melbourne Cup on Nov. 3, with Point of Law winning the 166th running of the 2-mile classic.
REC Equine Specialists managing partner Dr. Jonathan Lumsden issued a statement saying So You Are had been "humanely euthanized under anesthesia" after receiving emergency treatment.
"After his death, So You Are was collected by our contracted service provider and taken to a licensed landfill. He should have been promptly and respectfully buried," Lumsden said. "What happened was unacceptable and disrespectful to So You Are and to everyone who cared for him. We are deeply sorry."
Lumsden said he was working with the service provider and the state's horse racing authority, Racing NSW, to establish what went wrong and to put in processes to ensure it never happens again.
"So You Are was in our care. We did not carry out the burial ourselves, but we chose the provider and the arrangements, and we take full responsibility for that," he said. "We should have known exactly how horses were handled after leaving our hospital, and we did not. That process is not good enough, and it must change.
"No owner should have to go through what So You Are's connections have experienced this week."
Waste management company Cleanaway, which runs the landfill, told national broadcaster ABC the horse's body was moved to a permitted area of the site.
"Cleanaway's Lucas Heights landfill is licensed to accept and dispose of animal carcasses," a spokesperson told ABC. "The horse carcass delivered to the facility arrived in a small tipper truck, which is not permitted on the landfill tipping face for safety reasons. In accordance with established procedures, the carcass was transferred into a skip bin to enable its safe disposal at the landfill."
Racing NSW said So You Are was being held temporarily, awaiting burial, when the video was recorded.
"These images are distressing for all involved and for all of us who care deeply about our horses," Racing NSW said in a statement. "The way in which So You Are's body was left is distressing and completely unacceptable. So You Are deserved to be treated with dignity and respect."
The state's racing regulator said under industry guidelines — now under review — a licensed landfill was the preferred option for animals that have been euthanized because of the chemicals involved in the process.
"That burial, however, should have occurred in a timely and respectful manner," the statement continued. "If through the course of our ongoing investigation any wrongdoing is found, Racing NSW will not hesitate to take appropriate action."
Australian politician Emma Hurst called the news "absolutely heartbreaking," but not surprising, ABC reported.
"This horse has been treated as though he is nothing more than a piece of rubbish," she said. "To be completely honest, I'm not entirely surprised. We've had complaints about the racing industry for the entire eight years that I have been in parliament."

articles.title_orig: Trump admin. unveils new rule to deny China's access to U.S. AI chips
articles.title_zh: Trump admin. unveils new rule to deny China's access to U.S. AI chips
articles.content_orig:
United States President Donald Trump’s administration has announced new restrictions on China’s access to advanced chips amid fallout from the alleged spy scandal involving AI giant Nvidia.
The rule announced by the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) on Monday aims to prevent Chinese AI developers from getting around export controls by remotely accessing data centres in third countries, particularly in Southeast Asia.
It designates Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil as countries with an “unacceptable risk of diversion” and requires anyone seeking to ship advanced chips to those destinations to obtain an export licence.
BIS, which sits under the Department of Commerce, said the change was a “logical extension” of the existing requirement for companies to obtain a licence to export or transfer chips to firms based in China.
“The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten US national security,” BIS said in a statement.
While Chinese firms are barred from importing the most advanced graphics processing units (GPUs) under US export controls, they had until now been legally able to take advantage of remote access to top-of-the-line computing power at data centres in countries such as Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand.
Singapore, which hosts dozens of data centres, said on Tuesday that it was “studying the details of this new measure carefully”.
“We are engaging affected companies to understand the potential impact on their businesses,” the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry and the Ministry of Digital Development and Information said in a joint statement.
“We have also been engaging the relevant US authorities on the scope and implementation of the measure, as well as exploring how to facilitate trusted access for Singapore companies.”
The ministries added that they did not condone companies using Singapore to “circumvent or violate” the laws of other countries.
The restrictions come as Nvidia’s export of advanced chips is under scrutiny following claims that former CEO Jensen Huang was romantically involved with a woman recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security for espionage.
Huang, who became one of the most prominent faces of the AI boom at the helm of Nvidia, resigned last week amid a company board investigation into allegations involving the Chinese-born executive of Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.
Beijing has denied the spying allegations, made by unnamed US officials in media reports, calling them “entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China”.
Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive identified as Jensen Huang’s ex-romantic partner, has not publicly commented on the claims.
Late on Monday, the US Commerce Department and the Department of Justice publicly confirmed that investigators had opened a criminal investigation into Megaspeed.
The Commerce Department began investigating Megaspeed for potential export control violations in 2024, leading BIS officials to conduct an on-site inspection of the Singapore-based company and to interview Alice Huang the following year, the statement said.
The Justice Department subsequently took the “lead role” in the criminal investigation, according to the statement.
“The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred,” it said.
US tech stocks fell sharply on Monday as investors weighed the scandal’s fallout on the AI rollout.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 2.5 percent, closing in the red for the third consecutive session.
The broader S&P 500 dropped 1.9 percent.
Shares of Nvidia, which have shed more than 30 percent of their market value over the past month, dropped 4.1 percent.
The other six companies of the “Magnificent Seven” also lost ground, with Alphabet and Amazon seeing the next-biggest declines of 4.1 percent and 3.3 percent, respectively.
The sell-off continued in Asia on Tuesday, with key indexes in Japan, South Korea and Hong Kong closing in the red.
Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 and South Korea’s Kospi closed down 1.3 percent and 2.6 percent, respectively, while the Hang Seng Index in Hong Kong dropped 0.9 percent.

articles.content_orig:

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Taiwan is likely to be overshadowed as presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week, even as the threat from China evolves and grows stronger.
Leaders from China, the U.S. and some 21 other economies will gather at the APEC summit this week in Shenzhen, China. Recent events like the scandal that forced Nvidia's CEO to resign, export controls and the ongoing trade dispute have made the tech competition between Beijing and Washington all the more pressing.
Few expect major breakthroughs on Taiwan, a self-ruled island that is claimed by Beijing. While the U.S. does not formally recognize Taiwan, it is the island’s biggest informal ally and seller of arms.
“For the Trump administration, this isn’t a core issue between the U.S. and China,” said Arthur Zhin-Sheng Wang, an expert on cross-Straits relations at Taiwan’s Central Police University.
US-Taiwan ties remain strong behind the scenes
Experts largely say that cooperation with the U.S. remains strong below the level of rhetoric, despite Trump’s public ambivalence toward Taiwan.
One sign of this came from the summer, when the de facto United States embassy in Taiwan posted a photo showing joint patrols between the two coast guards, a rare occurrence, as the U.S. does not usually acknowledge it has direct cooperation with Taiwan in any defense capacity.
“This also is proof of the decades that Taiwan and U.S. have had of cooperation and training. I was also surprised,” said Kuo Yu-jen, a defense studies expert and director of the Institute for National Policy Research in Taiwan.
The U.S. is obligated by law to help Taiwan defend itself, which has manifested in the form of arms sales, while the government officially adopts a stance of ambiguity on whether it would intervene militarily in the case of a Chinese invasion.
The Taiwanese public is used to the continued uncertainties of the island’s relationship with the U.S. Research from the Institute of National Defense and Security Research in Taiwan, a government-funded think tank, showed that public attitudes toward the U.S. remain around the same. Polls conducted in the past five years show that about half of the public believes the U.S. will send soldiers to support Taiwan in the event of a Chinese invasion, and about half don’t.
“I do think they will take some actions, though it may not be sending soldiers,” said Allen Hsieh, a 28-year-old media professional in Taipei. “I think Taiwan’s importance to the U.S. is even more important than Ukraine.”
Stalled arms sales for now
Since starting his second term, Trump called for Taiwan to spend more on its own defense and Taiwan responded that it would commit to 5% of its GDP on defense.
Arms sales are ongoing. While much media attention has focused on a $14 billion package that remains stalled, an earlier package of $11 billion approved at the end of last year is in progress. Some of the stalled arms packages have been delayed since before Trump came into office, experts have also said.
Those include fighter jets. Taiwan received the first two of long-delayed F-16V fighter jets from the U.S. in October, and three more jets earlier this month. The aircraft are a part of a long list of backlogged U.S. orders worth almost $30 billion, according to the Taiwan Security Monitor research project which tracks defense-related developments on the island at George Mason University.
But the delays are not necessarily because of political considerations with China, a concern that was raised when Trump said he discussed arms sales with Xi earlier this year. Instead, it may be more of an issue with manufacturing capacity, particularly for future sales.
Congress approved the sale of long-range precision strike systems to Taiwan in December 2025, but Taiwan faces competition because of limited supplies. Kuo noted that among the missiles approved for sale are the same ones being used by the U.S. military in the ongoing Iran war, such as the HIMARS rockets and supplies were low.
“I don’t think this is a political issue. They just can’t produce so many of these missiles in a short period,” he said.
China expands coast guard role in pressure on Taiwan
Meanwhile, China has intensified its military and nonmilitary pressure on Taiwan. In 2025, the People’s Liberation Army flew about 5,448 fighter jet sorties toward the island during military exercises, according to Skyfaring, an open-source website that compiles public data from Taiwan’s Ministry of Defense. That marked a sharp increase from the years before 2023, when such flights were sporadic.
Beijing also recently held unannounced military drills in the Western Pacific, deploying more than 100 vessels in waters near Taiwan and Japan, Taiwan’s National Security Council chief Joseph Wu said in a Nov. 3 post on X.
The number of PLA flights recorded this year stood at 2,401 as of Nov. 12, below the full-year total for 2025.
“I think the threat is transforming ... for example, more of its exercises are now about blockading and sealing off” Taiwan, Wang said, rather than firing live missiles. He said Beijing was expanding its gray-zone tactics — aggressive actions that fall short of open warfare.
These include greater use of the coast guard to assert China’s claims, mirroring its approach elsewhere. In June, the Chinese coast guard began patrolling off Taiwan’s east coast, which faces the open Pacific, extending its activities beyond Taiwan’s outlying islands closer to China.
Wang compared the approach to Beijing’s tactics in the South China Sea, where Chinese coast guard vessels patrol waters disputed with the Philippines. China has also designated a shoal claimed by the Philippines as a nature reserve under Chinese protection.
“It’s telling the whole world it has sovereignty here.”
